Office of Zoning and Administrative Appeals hearings on the conditional-use modification scheduled for Sept 10-11, 2026.

The Office of Zoning and Administrative Hearings lists the hearing on case CU 24-13(a)(A) (Atmosphere Dickerson Property Owner, LLC; conditional use holder Terra Energy, LLC) as scheduled for Thursday and Friday, November 12 and 13, 2026, at 9:30 a.m.

projects.name: Project Double Reed (Stream US Data Centers at STAMP)
projects.note: Stream US Data Centers proposes a $19.46 billion, three-building, roughly 600 MW data center campus at the STAMP site in the Town of Alabama, Genesee County. The Town Planning Board reviewed site-plan conditions (annual noise monitoring, heat-island mitigation, a dedicated code enforcement officer) and was expected to vote July 6, but both July meetings were cancelled after GCEDC, the SEQRA lead agency, could not complete environmental-review documentation; the next scheduled Planning Board meeting was Aug 3, 2026. GCEDC's CEO says the project keeps moving unless New York's passed-but-unsigned statewide data center moratorium becomes law.

events.summary: A GCEDC public hearing was held February 3, 2025 on the original Stream/Project Double Reed incentive proposal at STAMP, ahead of staff bringing a recommendation to the STAMP committee and full board.
The GCEDC Board of Directors approved the original 900,000-square-foot, 250-megawatt Project Double Reed data center plan for Stream U.S. Data Centers at STAMP on March 6, 2025.

The Tonawanda Seneca Nation and the Sierra Club filed suit in New York State Supreme Court alleging GCEDC violated SEQRA by awarding $472 million in subsidies to Stream U.S. Data Centers without conducting a full environmental review or requiring detailed project plans.

The GCEDC board voted to withdraw the State Environmental Quality Review determination for the approved 900,000-square-foot project after Stream said it had identified an opportunity to secure additional capacity and increase the project's scale, with Stream to submit an amended, larger application; a Tonawanda Seneca chief called the withdrawal a win.

Stream submitted a revised GCEDC SEQR application dated February 18, 2026 increasing the campus to a $19.46 billion, roughly 500 MW, 2.2 million-square-foot three-building project on about 90 acres, with roughly 125 permanent jobs.

At a March 31, 2026 meeting, a Wendel Companies engineer walked the Town of Alabama Planning Board through the Stream site plan (water, sanitary sewer, noise studies, generators, roads, emergency services, parking); the board made no decisions and scheduled a public hearing for April 20 at the Alabama Fire Department.

The Alabama Planning Board held a public hearing on the $19.46 billion Stream project at the Alabama Fire Hall with almost 75 speakers, a majority opposed over noise, water, wetlands and impacts near the Tonawanda Seneca Nation, while some trades union representatives supported it; Stream design manager Colm Curran presented the project.

On June 2, 2026, Wendel Companies engineers updated the Alabama Planning Board on draft site-plan conditions dated May 26, 2026 covering annual noise readings, construction traffic routes, a heat-island memorandum, stormwater, grading, utilities and safety; the board chair said there was no deadline for a decision.

Alabama Planning Board met for over 3.5 hours on the Stream site plan amid resident opposition; conditions discussed included lifetime annual noise monitoring and a one-year construction-start deadline, with a site-plan approval vote expected July 6.
Town supervisor announced the July 6 and July 20 Planning Board meetings were cancelled - GCEDC could not complete SEQRA documentation in time - with the next regular meeting set for Aug 3, 2026.

The Tonawanda Seneca Nation and the Sierra Club filed a lawsuit in New York State Supreme Court seeking to invalidate the zoning agreement between the Town of Alabama and the GCEDC that underpins development at the STAMP industrial park.

Governor Kathy Hochul signed an executive order on July 14, 2026 establishing New York's first statewide moratorium of up to one year, pausing the Department of Environmental Conservation from issuing discretionary environmental permits for new hyperscale data centers while the state builds a regulatory framework and Community Investment Framework.

On July 29, 2026 Governor Hochul held a roundtable in Henrietta defending the one-year data center moratorium she signed July 14, saying New York does not need to be first but wants to be the first to get it right and that developers should bear infrastructure costs; coverage tied the pause to Stream's proposed $19.5 billion STAMP campus in the Town of Alabama.

projects.name: Stonebridge Associates data center campus at Powder Mill Works
projects.note: Maryland-based Stonebridge Associates has applied to build a data center campus at the Powder Mill Works commercial development site spanning North Beaver and Mahoning townships in Lawrence County, PA. The application was rejected administratively because a required $3,000 Lawrence County escrow check was missing, and back-to-back zoning hearings in early August 2026 argued over whether the application was validly filed - which determines whether older April or newer June zoning rules apply. The zoning board deferred its ruling, expected within 45 days.

events.summary: Mahoning Township Board of Supervisors passed a data center zoning ordinance restricting data centers to industrial districts, despite significant resident opposition at a packed public hearing; supervisors also authorized a noise and vibration study.

S.S. Penn LLC (Stonebridge affiliate) delivered a box of preliminary land development plans to Mahoning Township for a 15- to 16-building data center campus on 568-569 acres at the Powder Mill Works site, along with checks to Mahoning Township and Lawrence County but missing the required $3,000 county escrow fee.

Mahoning Township Board of Supervisors passed three additional ordinances regulating data centers, power generation, and battery storage in industrial districts, tightening setback, noise, and vibration restrictions beyond the April ordinance.

New Castle News reported the preliminary land development plan by S.S. Penn LLC for 16 buildings on 569 acres at the Powder Mill Works site; planning commission reviews were scheduled for early July in both townships and Lawrence County.

Stonebridge principal Douglas Firstenberg presented data center plans to approximately 40 residents at a North Beaver Township planning commission meeting, projecting 400-500 permanent jobs, over $1 billion investment, and $10 million annual tax revenue for Mahoning Township.

Attorney Louis Perrotta, representing both townships, announced he would file motions to quash lawsuits brought by S.S. Penn LLC challenging the timing of revised zoning ordinance amendments; a hearing was set before Judge Bradley Olson in Lawrence County Common Pleas Court.

Data Center Dynamics reported Stonebridge plans to invest over $15 billion on the 16-building campus at the former dynamite factory site, with Penn Power providing electricity and a six-year build-out; a petition against the project had gathered 170 signatures.

WFMJ reported Stonebridge is suing both North Beaver and Mahoning townships, arguing zoning restrictions adopted after it submitted its plans should not apply under the pending-ordinance doctrine; township solicitor Perrotta contended the application was incomplete and underfunded.

Approximately 150 residents packed a Stonebridge public meeting in New Castle, chanting opposition; Firstenberg outlined 16 buildings over six years, 3,000 construction and 400 permanent jobs, a 2029 construction start, and potential tenants Meta, Oracle, and Amazon AWS (none confirmed).

WFMJ reported residents voiced strong frustration at the Stonebridge public presentation in New Castle, with attendees demanding design plans and criticizing the company's claims about health and environmental impacts.

North Beaver Township held a zoning hearing on the Stonebridge application, focusing on whether fees were paid correctly and whether the application was timely; Stonebridge lawyer Shawn Gallagher said if the June regulations apply rather than April's, the company 'might not have a project.'

Second zoning hearing (Mahoning Township) on whether Stonebridge's application was filed correctly and on time; the filing had been rejected over a missing $3,000 county escrow fee, and the board deferred its decision, indicating a ruling within 45 days.

projects.name: Prime Data Centers — Starpointe Business Park campus
projects.note: Prime Data Centers filed a conditional-use application in May 2026 for a seven-building, ~1.7 million sq ft data center campus with an attached behind-the-meter 450 MW gas-fired power plant on roughly 126 acres of reclaimed strip-mine land in the Starpointe Business Park (land owned by ALTIAN Development LLC), near the Pavilion at Starlake. The Aug. 5 conditional-use hearing drew 200+ residents; about three dozen won party status, and residents' attorneys argued the application belongs before the zoning hearing board rather than the supervisors, so the hearing was continued to Aug. 31 without Prime presenting.

events.summary: Prime Data Centers LLC filed a conditional-use application in May 2026 for a seven-building data center with an attached power generation facility in the Starpointe Business Park.
Hanover Township adopted an ordinance regulating data center development during a meeting in March 2026, before Prime Data Centers LLC submitted its Starpointe application.

CBS Pittsburgh reported that residents were mounting an 11th-hour fight against the proposed Starpointe data center ahead of the Aug. 5 hearing, citing health concerns from infrasound, noise and emissions and criticizing the township's data center ordinance as insufficiently protective on setbacks and noise.

Conditional-use hearing before Hanover Township supervisors drew hundreds of residents; roughly three dozen were granted party standing, and residents' attorneys argued the zoning hearing board must first determine the data center's comparable use, so the hearing was continued to Aug. 31.
Continued conditional-use hearing scheduled for 6 p.m. at the Hanover VFD Firehall.

projects.name: 900 Conshohocken Road data center (former Cleveland-Cliffs steel mill)
projects.note: 900 Conshohocken Road LLC, an entity of developer Brian O'Neill, seeks a special exception from Plymouth Township's zoning hearing board to convert the recently closed Cleveland-Cliffs steel mill — 10 existing buildings totaling about 2 million sq ft on 66 acres along the Schuylkill River — into a data center. The Aug. 6 hearing nearly filled a 750-seat auditorium; Conshohocken Borough was granted party status while Norristown was denied. The board set a procedural-only session for Aug. 17, with testimony continuing in September; an opposition petition has topped 4,000 signatures.

events.summary: The Plymouth Township Planning Agency voted 4-0 not to recommend a special exception to allow a data center at 900 Conshohocken Road.

A resident petition opposing the proposal had reached more than 400 signatures, led by Patricia Smith, citing environmental, proximity, and utility-cost concerns; the article noted the Cleveland-Cliffs mill was scheduled to close the following month.

A zoning hearing ended abruptly Monday night when the developer withdrew its application; the township solicitor said the applicant lacked legal standing because the agreement of sale had not been finalized.

Plymouth Township announced it had received a resubmitted zoning application from an entity tied to developer Brian O'Neill seeking a special exception for a data center in the Heavy Industrial district at 900 Conshohocken Road.

Plymouth Township Council issued a formal statement setting out its perspective on the proposed 900 Conshohocken Road data center and the zoning proceedings, and noted the public hearing set for June 25 at Colonial Middle School.

The zoning hearing kicked off at Colonial Middle School focused on procedural matters; party status was granted to Plymouth Township, the property owner's representatives, nearby residents, and the Borough of Conshohocken Authority, with no testimony taken.

Council Chair Lynne Viscio accused developer Brian O'Neill of bullying, saying the township would not be bullied or intimidated; O'Neill called the accusations a 'bold-faced lie,' and he challenged the validity of the township's zoning ordinance.

Zoning hearing board session at Colonial Middle School drew a nearly full 750-seat auditorium; the applicant's engineer began testimony comparing the data center to permitted heavy-industrial uses, and party-status requests from neighboring municipalities and residents were taken up.

At the Zoning Hearing Board session, residents booed and cursed as a witness testified data centers resemble manufacturing; the board rejected several legal motions filed by opponents and indicated it would continue the case in September.
Hearing continued to Aug. 17 for procedural matters only, with no witness testimony; further testimony to be scheduled.

projects.name: AWS Salem Township campus (Susquehanna nuclear plant)
projects.note: One of two initial sites in Amazon's announced $20B+ Pennsylvania data-center investment: a campus alongside the Susquehanna Steam Electric Station nuclear plant, where majority owner Talen Energy agreed to supply 960 MW. The original behind-the-meter connection drew FERC scrutiny and was blocked in 2024. The 960 MW figure is the contracted power supply, not built capacity.

events.summary: Talen Energy disclosed in an investor presentation that AWS acquired the 1,200-acre Cumulus data center campus co-located with the Susquehanna nuclear plant for $650 million ($350M at closing, $300M escrowed pending zoning milestones), with plans to develop up to 960 MW.

Salem Township supervisors voted to rezone approximately 1,582 acres into a new industrial Special Data Center Overlay District, enabling AWS to build up to 15 data center buildings; the township also agreed to a 10-year LERTA tax break at a 70 percent discount for Amazon.

PJM Interconnection filed with FERC for an amended interconnection service agreement to increase behind-the-meter power delivery from the Susquehanna nuclear plant to the co-located AWS data center from 300 MW to 480 MW.

American Electric Power and Exelon filed a protest with FERC challenging the amended ISA, arguing the co-location deal could shift up to $140 million in annual transmission costs onto other PJM ratepayers.
Talen Energy announced that the $300 million escrowed portion of the Cumulus campus purchase price was released after completion of zoning milestones allowing development of the AWS campus to 960 MW.

FERC voted 2-1 to reject the amended interconnection service agreement that would have increased behind-the-meter power from Susquehanna to the AWS data center from 300 MW to 480 MW, finding PJM failed to justify the departure from its standard agreement.
FERC issued an order deferring Talen Energy's November 20, 2024 rehearing request on the Susquehanna ISA rejection, stating it would address the request in a future order.

Talen Energy filed suit in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit challenging FERC's November 2024 order rejecting the behind-the-meter interconnection agreement for the AWS data center at Susquehanna.

FERC upheld its rejection of the amended interconnection service agreement between PJM and Susquehanna Nuclear on rehearing, reaffirming its November 2024 order blocking expanded behind-the-meter power sales to the AWS data center.

Spotlight PA reported in June 2025 that Amazon's data centers qualify for Pennsylvania's sales tax exemption on data center equipment (enacted 2016, expanded 2021), with the state projecting $43 million in lost revenue for fiscal year 2025-26; critics noted no mandatory reporting of exempt transaction costs.

Amazon and Gov. Shapiro announced at least $20 billion for data center campuses in Pennsylvania, with initial sites in Salem Township (alongside the Susquehanna nuclear plant, with Talen Energy agreeing to provide 960 MW) and Falls Township, creating at least 1,250 permanent jobs.

Talen Energy and Amazon finalized a restructured 17-year, $18 billion power purchase agreement supplying up to 1,920 MW from Susquehanna via a grid-connected front-of-meter retail structure, bypassing the rejected behind-the-meter model; deliveries to ramp to 840-1,200 MW by 2029 and 1,680-1,920 MW by 2032.

FERC argued in an October 2025 brief to the Fifth Circuit that Talen's lawsuit should be dismissed as moot because the company had already contracted to abandon the behind-the-meter co-location arrangement at issue in the appeal.

QTS (owned by Blackstone) completed acquisition of approximately 1,700 acres from 96 Salem Township landowners for over $500 million, planning a 12-to-17 building data center campus adjacent to the AWS site using water-free cooling technology.

projects.name: AWS Falls Township campus (Keystone Trade Center)
projects.note: Second initial site of Amazon's $20B+ Pennsylvania investment: a data center at NorthPoint Development's Keystone Trade Center (1,800-acre former U.S. Steel Fairless Works site), including conversion of a planned 1M sq ft distribution building on a 247-acre parcel at 1 Ben Fairless Drive and a broader ~2M sq ft, 10-structure digital infrastructure campus. Falls Township supervisors approved revised preliminary/final land development plans for the data center use in March 2025.

events.summary: Falls Township announced Amazon will open a data center at the NorthPoint Development Keystone Trade Center site as part of Amazon's $20 billion Pennsylvania investment, with 1,250 jobs expected locally.

In March 2025, Falls Township supervisors approved revised preliminary and final land development plans converting the planned Building 6 distribution center at 1 Ben Fairless Drive to data center use.

projects.name: Social Circle data center complex (Fairplay Drive / Roy Malcom Road tracts)
projects.note: A data center complex assembled from three tracts totaling more than 450 acres on the southeast side of Fairplay Drive and Roy Malcom Road, from Social Circle Parkway to Hawkins Academy Road. The Social Circle Planning Commission voted unanimously at a called April 2026 meeting to recommend annexation, rezoning, special-use permitting and a future land use map change for the final 123-acre tract at 1402 Roy Malcom Road (concept plan: two buildings of about 248,600 sq ft each); the city council then approved all four requests 3-0 at a meeting reported May 1, 2026. Engineering firm Thomas & Hutton represents the property owner; project representatives say an unnamed 'end user' is already lined up and construction could begin in fall 2026.

events.summary: Council approved a special-use permit for a data center on a 181-acre tract along Fairplay Drive at Social Circle Parkway; councilmembers deadlocked 2-2 and Mayor David Keener broke the tie in favor. At the same meeting the council imposed a moratorium on new data center requests.

The data center moratorium ended when the council approved comprehensive new data center regulations, including noise and lighting limits, emergency drills, time limits on special-use permits, and special-use permitting even in heavy industrial zoning.

Annexation, rezoning, special-use and future land use map change requests were filed for the 123-acre tract at 1402 Roy Malcom Road, the first such filing considered under the city's new data center regulations.

projects.name: Project Red and Project Yellow
projects.filing_llc: National CRE Holdings LLC; Greenland Capital LLC
projects.note: Two proposed data center campuses covering 677 acres on the grounds of the existing Wolf Hollow power generating complex in Hood County. District Judge Bryan Bufkin of the 355th Judicial District Court granted the county's plea to the jurisdiction and dismissed with prejudice the developers' suit arguing the projects were automatically approved because the county missed a 30-day statutory deadline; the judge found the submissions did not meet the state's definition of 'development plans.' Commissioners had twice delayed voting on the projects pending more disclosure and compliance with new county development regulations. Reporting identifies National CRE Holdings LLC as a Starwood Capital Group entity and Greenland Capital LLC as the owner of MARA Holdings, which already operates two bitcoin mining sites in the county.

events.summary: Hood County Commissioners Court rejected a proposed six-month moratorium on new data center and industrial permits in a 3-2 vote; County Judge Massingill and Commissioners Andrews and Wilson voted against, Commissioners Samuelson and Eagle voted in favor.

State Sen. Paul Bettencourt and State Rep. Jared Patterson sent a letter to Attorney General Ken Paxton shortly before the moratorium vote urging him to investigate counties seeking data center moratoriums, arguing counties lack constitutional authority to issue them.

Hood County Commissioners Court rejected a second data center moratorium proposal in a 3-2 vote with the same split; commissioners voted instead to request a formal opinion from Attorney General Ken Paxton on whether the county has legal authority to enact such a ban.

Hood County Commissioners unanimously adopted amended Section One Development Permit Regulations requiring data center developers to demonstrate committed water resources, submit complete power generation concept plans, certify compliance with the Lone Star Infrastructure Protection Act, and limit building coverage to 10% of a property (down from 50%).

Hood County Commissioners unanimously voted to postpone action on the Project Red and Project Yellow concept plans pending receipt of additional information; the meeting revealed MARA Holdings' connection to both developments through a joint venture with Starwood, and residents raised concerns about environmental impacts and noise from existing MARA bitcoin mining operations.

The Texas Tribune reported that Hood County faces eight proposed data center projects spanning over 7,600 acres, including the 677-acre Project Red and Project Yellow on grounds neighboring the Wolf Hollow power plants; commissioners had twice delayed voting on those two projects pending more disclosure, prompting the developers to sue claiming automatic approval.
National CRE Holdings LLC and Greenland Capital LLC filed notice of appeal of Judge Bufkin's dismissal to the Second Court of Appeals.

District Judge Bryan Bufkin of the 355th Judicial District Court granted Hood County's plea to the jurisdiction and dismissed with prejudice the lawsuit by National CRE Holdings LLC and Greenland Capital LLC, ruling their concept plan submissions did not meet the statutory definition of 'development plans' that would trigger automatic approval under the 30-day deadline.

projects.name: Vantage Frontier
projects.note: Vantage Data Centers' largest campus and investment to date: a $25 billion, 1.4 GW AI campus on 1,200 acres in Shackelford County, Texas, comprising 10 data centers totaling 3.7 million square feet. Construction was already underway at announcement, with the first building scheduled for delivery in the second half of 2026 and more than 5,000 construction and operations jobs projected. Vantage says the campus uses liquid cooling with a closed-loop chiller system requiring minimal water. No tenant is identified in the announcement.

events.summary: Shackelford County Commissioners Court unanimously approved creation of Reinvestment Zone 2025-1, accepted Vantage's Chapter 312 tax abatement application, and declared intent to enter a formal agreement providing $10 million annual payments in lieu of property taxes for 10 years, plus $150,000 annually in charitable contributions.

The Albany News reported that Shackelford County commissioners approved the reinvestment zone and tax abatement application at a special meeting, with the formal agreement contingent on Vantage completing its land purchase within 30 days; up to 6,500 construction workers and 250 permanent jobs with $25 million annual payroll were projected.

KTAB Abilene reported County Judge John Viertel confirmed Vantage's $10 million annual payment deal, called it a significant uptick in the county's budget, and noted water concerns from residents regarding initial sourcing from Clear Fork Brazos River or Hubbard Creek Reservoir for the closed-circuit cooling system.
Vantage unveiled Frontier, a $25 billion, 1.4 GW, 1,200-acre, 10-building AI campus in Shackelford County, Texas, with construction underway and first delivery targeted for H2 2026.

OpenAI, Oracle, and SoftBank announced five new Stargate data center sites, identifying Shackelford County, Texas as one of three Oracle-partnered locations, as part of the $500 billion Stargate initiative targeting nearly 7 GW of new AI compute capacity.

Data Center Frontier reported the Shackelford County site as an extension of the Abilene area hosting Vantage's Frontier project, one of two Texas Stargate sites (alongside Milam County), both within ERCOT territory, as part of the push toward 10 GW total Stargate infrastructure.

The Albany News reported the Shackelford County data center received official confirmation as the Frontier Campus for Stargate, with Oracle's Mahesh Thiagarajan stating commitment to the Shackelford County community; the campus was specified as 700 acres with 1,600+ full-time positions upon completion.

Construction Owners reported that VoltaGrid will power the Frontier campus off-grid with 210 Jenbacher gas generators (197 prime, 13 backup) producing 700 MW in phase one, with TCEQ approval documented, representing one of the largest microgrid deployments in U.S. history.

VoltaGrid LLC submitted an application to TCEQ for Permit 182467, PSD Permit PSDTX1692, and GHG PSD Permit GHGPSDTX266 to construct an electric power generation facility using catalytically controlled four-stroke lean-burn engines at 299 FM 604, Abilene, Shackelford County.

Vantage Data Centers held a groundbreaking ceremony for the Frontier campus in Shackelford County as part of Oracle and OpenAI's Stargate expansion, with Kiewit confirmed as general contractor and the first facility scheduled for H2 2026 delivery and full completion by 2028.

KTXS reported Hamby residents seeking clarity on the Frontier campus water use; resident Lacie Rivera said residents were not consulted beforehand and called for a public meeting, while the City of Abilene declined on-camera interviews despite multiple requests.

Vantage Data Centers TX307 LLC registered TDLR project TABS2026024102 for a new 398,117 sq ft data center building (Building 7) at 246 PR 1604, Abilene, Shackelford County, with an estimated cost of $1.15 billion, construction start November 2026, and completion April 2028; Kiewit listed as contractor.

KTXS reported community concerns about a second proposed data center (Project North by Bolt Data and Energy) in Shackelford County, with residents questioning whether long-term benefits outweigh costs and citing heavy truck traffic from existing Frontier construction between Abilene and Hamby.

KTXS reported County Judge Viertel responded to backlash over the second proposed data center, acknowledging residents' overall view is resistance with water as the most prominent and legitimate concern, and saying any agreement would require accountability provisions.

The Texas Tribune reported Governor Abbott announced a moratorium on new data center grid connections pending PUCT and ERCOT audits of over 1,800 queued projects; the freeze does not apply to data centers with on-site power generation such as Frontier's behind-the-meter microgrid.

projects.name: AWS Madison County data center campuses
projects.note: AWS announced on 2024-01-25 a $10 billion investment and at least 1,000 jobs to build data center complexes in two Madison County industrial parks, then the largest capital investment in Mississippi history. On 2026-04-09 Amazon announced an additional $11 billion Madison County expansion and 700 more jobs, part of a $25 billion statewide total (also covering $3 billion in Warren County/Vicksburg and $1 billion at the former Delphi plant in Clinton, Hinds County) and more than 2,000 jobs. No per-campus megawatt or acreage figure is given in the sources fetched.

events.summary: Mississippi Development Authority announced AWS would invest $10 billion to establish data center complexes in two Madison County industrial parks, creating at least 1,000 jobs.
Governor Tate Reeves announced Amazon would add $11 billion and 700 jobs in Madison County, bringing Amazon's planned Mississippi investment to $25 billion and 2,000+ jobs.

projects.name: Monticello Tech data center campus
projects.note: Monticello Tech, led by Frattalone Companies CEO Nick Frattalone, filed a land-use application with the City of Monticello, Minnesota on 2026-07-07 seeking rezoning to a Data Center Planned Unit Development district plus preliminary plat and conditional use permit approvals for a site south of 85th Street NE and east of Highway 25. The application describes 547 acres (364 developable), up to 3 million sq ft, as many as 8 principal buildings, about 75,000 gallons/day of water, and a connection to Xcel Energy's 345 kV system; the developer projects about $7 million in annual property tax at full buildout, with construction possibly starting Q1 2028. The eventual operator is not identified. City staff had until 2026-08-21 to determine whether the application is complete; Minnesota law then allows a 60-day review, extendable to 120 days.

events.summary: The Monticello Planning Commission opened a public hearing on a proposed data center zoning ordinance (DCPUD) at the Mississippi Room of the Monticello Community Center, drawing large crowds.
The Monticello Planning Commission held a continued public hearing on the DCPUD zoning ordinance; the hearing closed without a vote and the ordinance was tabled.

In November 2025, the City of Monticello published the Draft Alternative Urban Areawide Review (AUAR) for a 550-acre industrial area and opened a 30-day public comment period running November 18 through December 18, 2025.

The Monticello City Council unanimously adopted the Final AUAR and Mitigation Plan for the 550-acre Monticello Industrial area, covering two development scenarios including a 3-million-square-foot technology campus.
The Monticello Planning Commission unanimously recommended approval of the DCPUD (Data Center Planned Unit Development) zoning ordinance to the City Council.

The Minnesota Center for Environmental Advocacy (MCEA) filed suit in Wright County District Court (Case No. 86-CV-26-1130) against the City of Monticello and Monticello Tech LLC, challenging the adequacy of the AUAR environmental review.
Close to 500 Monticello residents gathered at a local park to sign a statutory citizen petition seeking additional environmental review of the proposed Monticello Tech data center project.

The Monticello City Council approved the DCPUD zoning ordinance in a 4-1 vote, establishing setback, screening, infrastructure, and environmental standards for data center development; Council Member Charlotte Gabler cast the sole dissenting vote.
MPR News reported on the newly approved Monticello DCPUD ordinance, noting data centers face new restrictions while the ordinance opens the door to building in Monticello.

Wright County District Court Judge Suzanne Bollman issued a scheduling order in the MCEA v. Monticello lawsuit, setting discovery to conclude by October 15, 2026 and a pretrial conference for December 29, 2026.

Monticello Times reported that Monticello Tech was targeting a July application for its proposed data center site, with the city confirming no formal application had yet been submitted and pre-application discussions were ongoing.
Monticello Tech submitted its formal data center application to the City of Monticello, Minnesota, ahead of the Planning Commission's tentative Aug. 4 agenda.

The City of Monticello issued a nine-page letter deeming Monticello Tech's July 6 land-use applications incomplete, citing inconsistencies in applicant information, missing survey certifications, incomplete project narratives, and absent engineering and environmental documentation.

Monticello Tech submitted a revised application with hundreds of pages of engineering plans and technical studies, detailing a 547-acre campus (364 acres developable) with up to 3 million sq ft across eight buildings, air-cooled design using approximately 75,000 gallons of water daily, and an estimated $73.5 million in infrastructure costs funded by the developer.

projects.name: Antelope Data Campus (Project Antelope)
projects.note: Iron County Planning Commission unanimously approved a conditional use permit on 2026-06-04 for Pronghorn Development LLC's five-building campus (up to 6.75M sq ft, with an on-site natural gas plant of up to 1.5 GW) on 640 acres along Antelope Springs Road, about 8 miles west of Cedar City, with 62 conditions covering water rights, wastewater, noise, lighting and site restoration. The application was vested before a county moratorium on new data center applications adopted the month prior; additional permits are still required before construction. Buildout is proposed in phases over 8-10 years.

events.summary: Iron County Planning Commission held a public hearing in March 2025 on proposed Ordinance 2025-4, which would add Chapter 17.37 to the county land use code and amend the Table of Uses and Definitions to create provisions for permitting data centers.
Iron County Planning Commission held a public hearing on April 3, 2025 at Festival Hall in Parowan to receive public comment on proposed data center zoning amendments (Ordinance 2025-4).

Pronghorn Development LLC submitted a conditional use permit application in November 2025 for the 640-acre Antelope Data Campus, months after the county amended its zoning ordinance to allow data centers.

Iron County posted a public notice for a conditional use permit for a data center and data center power plant on 640 acres, scheduling a Planning Commission informational session for March 5 at Festival Hall in Cedar City (no action to be taken).
SUU News reported growing resident concerns ahead of the March 5 hearing, citing drought fears, potential utility price increases, and loss of farmland from the proposed 640-acre data center.

Approximately 350 residents packed Festival Hall in Cedar City for a Planning Commission hearing on the Antelope Data Center; over three hours of public comment were heard, with only one of more than 15 speakers expressing support, and concerns focused on water, air quality, noise, and wildlife.

KUTV reported the Antelope Data Center could bring 670 direct jobs and reduce Iron County property tax rates by approximately 55%; Commissioner Mike Bleak said he shifted from skepticism to support after touring existing facilities.

Baxtel reported plans had emerged for the 640-acre Antelope Data Center with five buildings totaling 1.35 million sq ft and an on-site 1.5 GW natural gas power plant; no formal action or public hearing occurred at a late-March Planning Commission meeting.

Iron County Commission adopted a 180-day moratorium (Ordinance 2026-13) on new data center, power plant, and solar plant applications to review zoning regulations; the existing Pronghorn application was exempted because it had already been deemed complete.

KJZZ reported the Antelope Data Center faced an uncertain path ahead of the June 4 Planning Commission vote; the commission could approve, deny, modify conditions, or continue the item, and Commissioner Bleak noted the project could still be several years from breaking ground.

Iron County Planning Commission unanimously approved a conditional use permit for the Antelope Data Campus with 62 conditions; the application was vested under existing ordinance ahead of the county's data center moratorium.

Utah Public Radio reported the Iron County Planning Commission unanimously approved the data center's conditional permit one week after the county paused all new applications; construction is planned over 8 to 10 years, and a 480-page impact report is publicly available.

The Salt Lake Tribune reported the Iron County Planning Commission approved the conditional use permit for the Antelope Data Center, which would include a 1.5-gigawatt natural gas power plant approximately 15 miles northwest of Cedar City.

KSL reported the unanimous approval of the Antelope Data Campus CUP for up to five buildings on 640 acres with phased construction over 8-10 years; Pronghorn Development stated the permit 'validates the trust we've built with our neighbors.'

Iron County Today reported the approval followed months of debate and a packed March public hearing; conditions included dozens of protections, and Planning Commission Chair Erick Cox said they did their 'very best to protect the people in Iron County.'

Pronghorn Development issued a press release via Utah Policy announcing it secured the conditional use permit for the 1.5 GW Antelope Data Campus, projecting thousands of construction jobs, hundreds of permanent positions, and billions in economic impact.

Spectrum & Daily News (SUNews) reported the approval cleared a major hurdle but noted additional permits and regulatory approvals are still required before construction can begin; Governor Cox's Executive Order 2026-03 was signed days before the June 4 vote.

projects.name: Stratos
projects.note: O'Leary Digital, chaired by Kevin O'Leary, proposes the Stratos campus in unincorporated Box Elder County near Brigham City: eleven 100 MW data center buildings plus a 7.5-9 GW natural gas plant and a 500 MW solar array on roughly 40,000 acres across three sites. Renderings were released 2026-05-19; the county commission approved an interlocal agreement with the Military Installation Development Authority in early May 2026. State environmental permitting could take about two years, with a 30-day public comment period and hearing required, and over 40 protests have been filed on its water rights application.

events.summary: MIDA's board of directors approved four resolutions and a tax ordinance creating the Stratos Project Area, before Box Elder County had formally consented; critics later alleged MIDA also signed a development agreement the same morning.

Box Elder County Commission approved Resolutions 26-11 and 26-12 consenting to the MIDA Stratos Project Area and an interlocal agreement, at a contentious meeting at the county fairgrounds in Tremonton with hundreds of opponents present and sheriff's deputies controlling the crowd.

The holder of an 1904-vintage water right withdrew a change application seeking to convert 1,900 acre-feet from agricultural to industrial use for the Stratos project, after more than 3,700 formal protests were filed at $15 each; the developer stated it fully intends to refile.

Utah House Speaker Mike Schultz said he did not attend the meeting Kevin O'Leary described on Fox News and only learned of the project in early April 2026; the Deseret News reported the project's estimated cost exceeds $100 billion.

Approximately 400 to 500 people rallied at the Utah Capitol against the Stratos project, delivering an opposition letter signed by over 7,500 people calling on Governor Cox, House Speaker Schultz, and Senate President Adams to order independent water and fiscal studies.

Grist reported the project would raise Utah's carbon emissions by 64 percent and that a physics professor calculated 16 gigawatts of waste heat could spike Hansel Valley nighttime temperatures by as much as 28 degrees Fahrenheit.

O'Leary Digital released renderings of the proposed Stratos campus in Box Elder County; state environmental approvals were estimated at roughly two years, with air monitoring required for one year before a permit application.
Hundreds of Utahns rallied at the state Capitol a second time demanding a halt to the Box Elder data center plan, calling on state leaders to protect water, air, and land.

Box Elder County Attorney Stephen Hadfield rejected three referendum applications challenging the May 4 commission vote, ruling the resolutions were irrevocable administrative actions rather than newly created laws and thus not referable to voters.
Governor Spencer Cox declared the Stratos project will 'never' run solely on natural gas, stating the first phase would use gas but subsequent phases should use nuclear, geothermal, and solar power.

Alliance for a Better Utah and five Box Elder County residents filed suit in Utah's 3rd District Court challenging MIDA's constitutionality and seeking to void the Stratos approval, also alleging Senate President Adams had a conflict of interest from a $135,000 PAC donation.

Box Elder Accountability Referendum (BEAR) filed an appeal in Utah 1st District Court in Brigham City challenging the county attorney's rejection of referendum applications on Resolutions 26-11 and 26-12, arguing the approvals were legislative acts subject to voter referendum.

O'Leary agreed to cut the project area from roughly 40,000 acres to 20,000 acres, removing the Locomotive Springs and I-84 parcels and keeping only the Hansel Valley parcel, with 10,000 acres designated as open space.

Box Elder County commissioners unanimously approved a 180-day moratorium on new data centers and power plants on unincorporated land, but explicitly exempted the Stratos project whose land-use authority had been transferred to MIDA for 50 years.
Kevin O'Leary said design work on the Stratos data center is 'full steam ahead' while MIDA remains on 'pause' awaiting permit requests for the project.

projects.name: QTS Cedar Rapids Data Center Campus
projects.note: QTS (a Blackstone portfolio company) is building a seven-building campus on 612 acres of Alliant Energy's Big Cedar Industrial Center; the Cedar Rapids City Council approved the development agreement with QTS Cedar Rapids LLC on 2025-01-28 with a minimum $750M investment, later announced by QTS as a $10B campus. The agreement includes up to $18M over 20 years to a Community Betterment Fund, tax increment financing rebates, and water-free cooling; the development agreement requires construction to begin within three years and finish within six.

events.summary: Cedar Rapids City Council approved a development agreement with QTS Cedar Rapids LLC for a minimum $750 million data center on 612 acres of the Big Cedar Industrial Center.
The City of Cedar Rapids, Alliant Energy and QTS announced the data center campus, described by the mayor as the largest economic development investment in the city's history.
QTS announced the Cedar Rapids campus as a $10 billion, seven-building development with water-free cooling and carbon-free energy sourcing in partnership with Alliant Energy.

projects.name: Compass Datacenters Red Oak campus
projects.note: Red Oak City Council voted 4-1 to rezone ~830 acres of agricultural land ~20 miles south of Dallas to a planned development for a Compass data center campus of nearly a dozen buildings plus substations, after a marathon May 11 meeting that ran past midnight with 150+ residents present and ~1,600 petition signatures against; the planning and zoning board had recommended denial in late April. Conditions include lighting shields, decibel limits, a cryptocurrency-mining ban, closed-loop cooling with no city water draw, and $72 million in electric grid reinforcements; a 10-year, $2.82 million tax abatement passed on a separate 4-1 vote.

events.summary: Compass Datacenters announced it purchased 225 acres in Red Oak, Texas for a second Dallas-area campus capable of delivering 350+ MW of IT load, with a 6 MW facility scheduled for Q2 2020 delivery.

Compass Datacenters acquired 375 additional acres of vacant agricultural land in Red Oak, with plans to construct up to sixteen buildings on the new property, which a broker called potentially one of the largest campuses in the country.
Ellis County and the City of Red Oak partnered with Compass Datacenters on a tax abatement for Phase 2 construction of the Red Oak campus, which would double production capacity.

Schneider Electric and Compass Datacenters announced a $3 billion five-year partnership to manufacture prefabricated modular data centers, including a 110,000 sq ft integration facility to be built adjacent to the Red Oak campus.

Schneider Electric held a ribbon cutting for its 105,000 sq ft data center integration facility adjacent to the Compass Red Oak campus, expected to create over 200 jobs and produce 240 power centers in 2025.

Compass Datacenters secured a $326 million refinancing (maturing 2050) on five fully leased hyperscale data centers at its Red Oak campus totaling 180 MW, with three additional facilities planned at a combined $300 million construction budget.

Red Oak's Planning and Zoning Commission voted 3-2 to recommend denial of the rezoning request for the proposed 830-acre Compass data center campus after a lengthy hearing with large community turnout.

Over 150 residents packed Red Oak City Hall (capacity 136, with 70+ waiting outside) for a marathon council meeting on the 830-acre Compass rezoning; public comment ran past 10 p.m. and the meeting lasted nearly five hours.

City council approved the rezoning 4-1 around midnight following the May 11 meeting, with a separate 4-1 vote approving a tax abatement; over 150 residents attended and the council held an hour-long executive session before voting.

KERA reported that on the same day Red Oak approved the Compass rezoning, Somervell County commissioners voted unanimously on a non-binding resolution to restrict future data centers, highlighting a regional divide over data center growth.

At least eight Red Oak residents received code violation notices for posting 'No Data Center' yard signs; after CBS Texas coverage, the city acknowledged citing the wrong code and closed all related cases.

Compass Datacenters announced a $15 million commitment to build a new Ellis County animal shelter, calling itself a '100-year neighbor'; the grant requires approval by the Ellis County Commissioners Court.

Compass Datacenters withdrew its county tax abatement request for the proposed 890-acre Red Oak property before the June 23 Ellis County Commissioners Court meeting, with CEO Chris Crosby citing growing community 'noise' around the project.

Compass Datacenters and Texas State Technical College held a ribbon cutting for a $12.6 million, 40,000 sq ft training facility on the Red Oak campus for the MEI Data Center Pathway Program, a 12-week curriculum for career changers.

The Waxahachie Sun reported that the nonprofit Say NO MORE Data Centers (rebranding as Save Our Red Oak) is financing a legal challenge to Red Oak data centers through car show fundraisers and has retained legal counsel.

CRE Daily reported Red Oak has seven data center sites at various stages with a projected $13 billion total investment expected to quadruple the city's taxable land value; Google, Compass, and DataBank each received 10-year tax breaks.

NBC DFW reported Red Oak residents are petitioning the state for a data center moratorium and that the Texas Senate Finance Committee examined tax incentives and oversight of the state's 138 data centers.

projects.name: BCG Cedar Creek Campus
projects.note: Black Chamber Partners (a BlackChamber Group affiliate) and co-developer Pacifico Energy plan a 2,842-acre data center campus at 382 Earl Callahan Road near Cedar Creek with a 710 MW gas-fired energy facility, a ~$2.2 billion investment with two 100% county tax-abatement applications under review; construction is estimated for September 2026 through October 2028. Neighboring property owners filed motions July 20 asking TCEQ to overturn two construction stormwater permits issued in mid-July.

events.summary: Pacifico's engineer submitted two mass-grading permit applications to Bastrop County (one for the data center campus, one for the power facility), both in preliminary review.

Pacifico Cedar Creek LLC filed an application with the Texas Comptroller for a JETI (Jobs, Energy, Technology and Innovation Act) agreement, listing a $2.2 billion investment, 25 permanent jobs and $6.2 million in annual payroll.

Community Impact published its first detailed report on the proposed 2,842-acre, $2.2 billion Cedar Creek data center and 710 MW gas power campus near Earl Callahan Road, with two 100% county tax-abatement applications under review.

Neighboring property owners (the Jenkins and Lewis families) filed motions asking TCEQ to overturn two construction stormwater permits issued to Black Chamber and Pacifico Energy for the BCG Cedar Creek Campus.

More than 100 residents attended a town hall at Bastrop's Hampton Inn and Suites, organized by the League of Independent Voters of Texas, calling for guardrails on data center development including the Cedar Creek projects; attorney Nick Lealos proposed a 'Bastrop Bill of Rights' framework.

A Bastrop County Commissioners Court public hearing was scheduled on proposed tax-abatement guidelines that would require companies to disclose environmental impacts and create at least 25 local jobs.

The Cool Down published a national report on bipartisan backlash against AI data centers in Bastrop County, noting Texas has overtaken Virginia as the world's largest data center market, with over 700 facilities potentially added in the next decade.

The Elgin Courier reported on the community-led town hall calling for greater data center oversight in Bastrop County, noting that the Pacifico Energy data center proposal remained under county review alongside the EdgeConneX campuses.
Bastrop County commissioners tabled a resolution requesting expanded county authority over large-scale industrial projects; it returns at the Aug 24 meeting, 9 a.m., Bastrop County Courthouse.

Community Impact reported that the Black Chamber stormwater permit lists an estimated construction period of September 1, 2026 through October 1, 2028 for the 304-acre BCG Cedar Creek Campus portion of the 2,842-acre development, and that TCEQ generally has 45 days to act on the motions to overturn or they are denied by default.

projects.name: Amazon Fort Stockton campus
projects.note: Amazon Data Services filed TDLR registrations for three data center buildings (A, B, C; 189,060 sq ft and ~$300 million each) at a site 11 miles north of Fort Stockton, with construction scheduled August-December 2026, part of an August 2026 filing wave totaling 16 buildings and at least $4.8 billion across Fort Stockton, Floydada, and Amazon's existing Boling (Wharton County) campus. Amazon confirmed it is financing the GW Ranch gas plant being developed by Pacifico Energy in Pecos County (35 turbines, 7.65 GW) to power the campus; its permitted emissions of over 30 million metric tonnes of GHG per year would exceed any single source currently operating in the US.

events.summary: Pacifico Energy announced the GW Ranch project, an off-grid power generation campus on 8,000+ acres in Pecos County combining natural gas turbines and battery storage to deliver 5 GW for hyperscale data centers, with 1 GW targeted for 2028 and full capacity by 2030.

Pacifico Energy announced it secured a TCEQ air permit for 7.65 GW of gas-fired power generation at GW Ranch, described as the largest air permit granted in the United States, with Phase 1 to deliver 1 GW in the first half of 2027.

The Big Bend Sentinel reported a massive AI data center campus coming to Pecos County on Highway 18 north of Fort Stockton, with Pecos County Judge Joe Shuster and Economic Development Director Remie Ramos expressing support for the project's economic benefits.

Pecos County Commissioners Court held a public hearing to designate and establish the GW Ranch Reinvestment Zone under Texas Tax Code Chapter 312 and considered approving a tax abatement agreement with Pacifico GW LLC.
Airbus satellite imagery captured on this date showed land clearing already underway at the GW Ranch site north of Fort Stockton, as reported by Cleanview on August 7.

Governor Greg Abbott announced a moratorium on new data center approvals pending an ERCOT and PUCT audit of energy, water, and community impacts; off-grid projects like Amazon's Pecos County campus were noted as largely unaffected since they bypass grid interconnection.

RFD-TV reported that Floyd County commissioners plan to use a Chapter 312 tax abatement agreement to impose conditions on a proposed Amazon data center campus valued at over $1 billion in Floydada, part of the same August 2026 Amazon filing wave that includes the Fort Stockton campus.
Amazon Data Services' TDLR filings for three 189,060 sq ft, ~$300M data center buildings 11 miles north of Fort Stockton were reported, with construction scheduled August-December 2026.

The New Republic reported that Amazon's GW Ranch gas plant in Pecos County, permitted for 33 million tons of CO2 annually, would be the biggest single pollution source in the United States, exceeding the nation's largest coal power plant.

Amazon confirmed it is financing the 7.65 GW, 35-turbine GW Ranch gas plant (developer Pacifico Energy) in Pecos County to power its new data center campus there, per reporting on Cleanview's analysis connecting Amazon's construction permits to the plant.

The San Antonio Current reported the Amazon campus on 8,400 acres along Highway 18, approximately 17 miles north of Fort Stockton, could become the nation's largest polluter, noting concerns about proximity to Big Bend National Park and Amazon's net-zero 2040 pledge.

E&E News by Politico reported on Amazon's off-grid gas plant in Pecos County, quoting Environment Texas executive director Luke Metzger warning that data centers will 'build gas plants and increase climate and local air pollution' rather than using cleaner grid electricity.
The Fort Stockton Pioneer published a report on community debate over the data center proposal's impact on Fort Stockton land, water, and future growth.

projects.name: Amazon Floydada campus
projects.note: Amazon Data Services filed TDLR registrations for three data center buildings (B, C, D; 189,060 sq ft and ~$300 million each) near Floydada, about 45 miles northeast of Lubbock, with construction planned August 2026 through April 2027. The filings were part of an August 2026 wave totaling 16 buildings and at least $4.8 billion across Floydada, a new Fort Stockton (Pecos County) campus, and six added buildings at Amazon's existing Boling (Wharton County) campus.

events.summary: All Ag News reported that Floyd County commissioners plan to use a Chapter 312 tax-abatement agreement as leverage over the proposed Amazon data center campus, citing limited regulatory and zoning authority over private property as the reason for turning to incentive conditions to protect water and power resources.

RFD-TV reported that Floyd County commissioners are considering a Chapter 312 tax-abatement agreement for the proposed Amazon campus (valued at over $1 billion, seven buildings across ~485 acres), with conditions requiring air-cooled systems to reduce groundwater demand and on-site electricity generation to avoid competing with local homes, farms, and businesses during shortages.
Amazon Data Services' TDLR filings for three 189,060 sq ft, ~$300M data center buildings near Floydada were reported, with construction planned August 2026-April 2027.

projects.name: Manse Technology Campus (formerly Project Blackjack)
projects.note: Gigawatt Development proposes a ~900-acre, multi-phase technology campus south of Carpenter Canyon Road along SR-160 at the south end of Pahrump Valley, pledging closed-loop cooling using under 300 acre-feet of water per year (~1.5% of the Pahrump Basin's annual yield) on water rights it already owns, with no tax abatements sought; the application predates the county's June 2026 temporary moratorium on new data center applications. The 'August vote' was on Nye County Bill 2026-11, a proposed ban on data centers in communities without elected town boards: at the Aug 4 commission meeting it did not come to a vote, and commissioners instead moved toward putting the question to voters, with a possible special election (earliest January 2027) to be discussed Aug 18.

events.summary: Manse Technology Campus LLC was formed as a Nevada limited liability company, the entity behind Gigawatt Development's proposed Pahrump data center campus.

Several dozen Pahrump residents rallied at the intersection of Highway 160 and Highway 372 as part of the AI Data Center National Day of Protest, citing concerns about the town's sole-source aquifer, electricity costs, and noise.

Pahrump resident Justyne Lobello hosted an 'AI and Data Centers: 101' educational presentation at the Pahrump Community Library at 1 p.m., drawing a large crowd of concerned residents amid the proposed data center development.
Manse Technology issued a press release announcing project details, describing an estimated $18.4 billion technology campus with no property tax abatements proposed.

Nye County held a town hall/forum on the proposed Manse Technology Campus at the commission building in Pahrump; a large crowd attended inside and outside the venue, with residents opposing the project chiefly over water use.
The Manse Technology Campus team scheduled a public informational meeting for August 3 at 6 p.m. at the Pahrump Nugget Events Center to present the project and take questions.

Nye County Bill 2026-11, a proposed ban on data centers in areas without elected town boards, did not come to a vote; Commissioner Jabbour successfully moved to pursue a ballot question instead, with a possible special election to be discussed Aug 18. Over 3,400 people signed a petition supporting the ban and hundreds attended, most speaking against data center development.

The Nye County Water District Governing Board held a roughly two-and-a-half-hour discussion on August 6 featuring a presentation on the proposed Manse Technology Campus by Russ Meads of Double M Construction.

projects.name: Monarch Data Center
projects.note: Lyon County commissioners voted 3-1 (Commissioner Hockaday opposed; Commissioner Cassinelli abstained) to approve the planned unit development rezoning for Copia Power's ~505-acre, 4.6 million sq ft, 1,000 MW Monarch campus in Mason Valley north of Yerington, which includes a 500 MW natural-gas backup plant and battery energy storage, after 6+ hours of comment from a mostly opposed crowd of nearly 300. The approval covers zoning only: final PUD/design approval, Nevada Division of Environmental Protection and State Engineer permits, and completion of Copia's land purchase remain, and tribal members vowed legal action over cultural resources and sacred sites.

events.summary: Lyon County Planning Commission voted 4-3 (Loomis, Irvin, Allan opposed) to advance the Monarch project to county commissioners; over 200 people participated and a strong majority spoke against it, including tribal members citing lack of Paiute consultation.

Lyon County commissioners approved the planned unit development rezoning 3-1 with one abstention after more than six hours of discussion with dozens of opposing commenters; final PUD filing (one-year deadline), state permits, and environmental approvals remain before construction.

projects.name: Green Data Socorro campus (New Mexico Tech land)
projects.owner: New Mexico Institute of Mining and Technology (proposed site)
projects.note: Green Data Centers CEO Jason Bak proposed a 10,000-acre campus on New Mexico Tech land west of M Mountain and north of Highway 60 outside Socorro, powered by a 10 GW solar array delivering ~2 GW of base-load power, with atmospheric water generation for a water-neutral design; it was unveiled March 25, 2026 at a Socorro Electric Cooperative board meeting. After a raucous May town hall, New Mexico Tech announced June 2 it would not move forward, saying it lacks sufficient contiguous, undeveloped parcels for the ~16-square-mile footprint. Socorro County commissioners then unanimously adopted a one-year moratorium on data centers and supporting infrastructure on June 9.

events.summary: Green Data Centers CEO Jason Bak presented the proposed 10,000-acre project at a Socorro Electric Co-op board meeting, in collaboration with New Mexico Tech.
New Mexico Tech announced it would not move forward with the proposed data center, citing insufficient contiguous, undeveloped parcels for the project's footprint.

Socorro County commissioners unanimously adopted a one-year moratorium on development of data centers and supporting infrastructure, and opened applications for a committee to evaluate potential regulations.

projects.name: Terra Nexus data center campus (316 Old Cheraw Highway)
projects.filing_llc: Terra Nexus Land Fund I, LLC
projects.note: Terra Nexus Land Fund I, LLC asked Rockingham to rezone ~165 acres at 316 Old Cheraw Highway from high-density residential (R-7) to conditional light industrial for a $1.2B, ~30-job data center campus — Richmond County's third. The Planning Board unanimously recommended approval on Aug 4; a City Council public hearing must precede any vote, but fetched coverage (as of Aug 13) gives no confirmed hearing date.

events.summary: Rockingham City Council unanimously approved the voluntary annexation and rezoning of 69.23 acres on Old Cheraw Highway (the Clontz property) from rural residential to high-density residential for a planned housing subdivision by Sage Equity.
Ben and Amber Moss petitioned Rockingham to annex their adjacent 93.305-acre parcel on Old Cheraw Highway, citing interest from an entity planning a residential subdivision.
Rockingham City Council approved the annexation and rezoning of the Moss property (93.305 acres on Old Cheraw Highway) from rural residential (R-20) to high-density residential (R-7).

The Rockingham Planning Board reviewed Terra Nexus Land Fund I, LLC's request to rezone ~165 acres at 316 Old Cheraw Highway from high-density residential to conditional light industrial and unanimously recommended that the City Council approve it.

Richmond County commissioners responded to resident data center concerns; Commissioner Andy Grooms noted the Old Cheraw Highway site falls under Rockingham city jurisdiction and said the county has no authority over it, adding he does not want additional data centers.

WSOC-TV reported neighbors are split on the proposed third data center for Richmond County at Old Cheraw Highway; NC state Rep. Ben Moss, who once owned the land, called for transparency and public discussion before any decision.

The Richmond County Daily Journal reported that the Rockingham City Council will schedule a public hearing on the Terra Nexus conditional rezoning request; city council cannot vote until after the hearing is held.

projects.name: 1155 Powers Ferry Place data center (Prime Storage site)
projects.note: Marietta City Council voted 5-2 on Aug 12, 2026 to approve rezoning for an 18 MW, 90,000 sq ft data center at Prime Storage's ~11-acre Powers Ferry Place property near I-75 and Delk Road — the city's second data center. Conditions include silencers on coolers/generators, an independent sound study, no connection to municipal water, and Prime Storage agreeing not to build data centers at its other Marietta sites. The application predated the six-month moratorium the council passed July 8.

events.summary: The Cobb Chamber of Commerce approved the Prime Group data center project in July 2026, according to Atlanta News First.

East Cobb News reported that a request to rezone 10.7 acres at 1155 Powers Ferry Place to allow an 18-megawatt data center in the existing Prime Storage building, with about 21,570 square feet of mission-critical space, was set to be heard by the city; the applicant's name was blacked out on the zoning application.

The council passed a six-month moratorium on new data center applications (through Dec. 31, 2026); the 18 MW Powers Ferry Place application, filed before the freeze took effect, was not covered by it.

At the July 8 council meeting, Councilwoman Cheryl Richardson moved to table the Powers Ferry Place data center proposal, citing noise and asking for a sound and light study plus additional buffer space; the proposal was tabled until August 12.

Atlanta Press Collective reported the Marietta Planning Commission voted 4-3 to recommend approval of the 1155 Powers Ferry Place data center rezoning, a shift from previous data center approvals that had passed unanimously, amid growing community opposition.

CRE Daily reported residents pushing back on Prime Group's plan, noting the Marietta Planning Commission had endorsed the project about a week before the council delayed its decision and imposed a six-month moratorium through December 31.
Community organizers, including the group Marietta BLU, scheduled a town hall for July 28 near the proposed data center site.

After more than two hours of public comment at a capacity meeting, the council approved the rezoning 5-2, with conditions including silencers, an independent sound study, site monitoring, and no municipal water/electricity connection.
During the Marietta City Council meeting some protesters were escorted out by police, and residents raised concerns about noise and environmental pollution, especially to the nearby Rottenwood Creek.

projects.name: Stillwater data center campus (Panhandle Road)
projects.note: Stillwater Development's 15-building, 3.5 million sq ft campus at 11760 Panhandle Road — 1.25 GW at full build, sited across from Michelle Obama Elementary and Eddie White Middle school traffic — was withdrawn at an Aug 6, 2026 council meeting after strong community opposition; plans were first filed in December 2025. The developer is pivoting to residential development, and Mayor Marci Fluellyn said the city will begin updating its zoning to prohibit data centers.

events.summary: The proposal for a 15-building, 3.5 million sq ft, 1.25 GW data center campus at 11760 Panhandle Road was withdrawn at a Lovejoy council meeting; developers are pursuing residential development for the site instead.
Lovejoy's mayor and council voted unanimously to proceed with rescinding the project's permit; Mayor Fluellyn said a withdrawal from the DRI process would follow the next day.

projects.name: Mason County hyperscale data center campus
projects.note: The Mason County Fiscal Court gave final approval on May 22, 2026 to rezone 28 properties (2,080 acres, A-2 agricultural to I-3 industrial) outside Maysville for a hyperscale data center campus; the application's development plan shows six data center buildings, three utility substations, and 15 detention ponds on ~1,975 net acres. The developer's identity remains undisclosed, and a legal challenge by residents group We Are Mason County was pending at approval.

events.summary: The joint planning commission scheduled public hearings for March 25-26 at Maysville Community and Technical College on the zoning map amendment to take 2,080 acres from A-2 agricultural to I-3 industrial for a six-building hyperscale data center campus with three substations.

The Mason County Fiscal Court gave final approval to rezone the 28 properties outside Maysville for data center construction; the company behind the project remains undisclosed and a We Are Mason County lawsuit over the process was pending.

projects.name: Baconton power generation facility (data-center-linked, NextEra-linked)
projects.note: On June 29, 2026 Mitchell County commissioners rezoned ~300 acres of agricultural land to industrial near Baconton, clearing the way for a 1,500 MW power generation facility linked in reporting to NextEra Energy and described by residents as intended to supply data centers across southwest Georgia — the rezoned project is a power plant, not a data center itself (size_mw is generation capacity). Residents are pursuing a referendum on the rezoning, a one-year data center moratorium petition, and recalls of commissioners.

events.summary: Mitchell County commissioners voted to rezone approximately 300 acres of agricultural land to industrial near Baconton, enabling a 1,500-megawatt power generation facility linked to NextEra Energy.
About 400 residents gathered at the American Legion to sign two petitions: a referendum on the power-generating facility and a one-year moratorium on all proposed data centers.
Recall organizers submitted the first 100 required signatures against District 5 Commissioner David Griner, the first formal step under Georgia's recall law.

projects.name: Cave City data center (Kentucky Industrial Alliance)
projects.note: Kentucky Industrial Alliance LLC proposes a data center on a 381-acre project site within its 600+ acres at 2001 Doyle Avenue, about 10 miles from Mammoth Cave National Park; it submitted an application May 11, 2026, and sued the city on June 8 after Cave City adopted a one-year moratorium. The city moved to dismiss on June 29, arguing no actual development plan was ever filed; a July 20 preliminary-injunction hearing was scheduled. Residents fear runoff through the karst into the Mammoth Cave system.

events.summary: Cave City Council approved the ordinance annexing approximately 245 acres of the former Branstetter property into the city limits, the land later tied to the proposed data center.
The Joint City-County Planning Commission unanimously approved proposed data center regulations during a public hearing and forwarded them to the Cave City Council.
Kentucky Industrial Alliance LLC submitted a development application for a data center on its 600+ acre property at 2001 Doyle Avenue in Cave City.
Cave City held the first of two special meetings regarding data centers.
Cave City held a second special meeting and subsequently enacted a 12-month moratorium on data centers.

Kentucky Industrial Alliance LLC sued Cave City, the City Council, and the Joint City-County Planning Commission in Barren County Circuit Court, arguing the one-year data center moratorium violates due process.
The Cave City Council voted to hire outside legal counsel to defend against Kentucky Industrial Alliance's lawsuit.
Cave City's attorneys filed a motion to dismiss, arguing the company never submitted an actual development plan under city ordinances.

Kentucky Industrial Alliance filed a second lawsuit in Barren Circuit Court seeking to void Cave City's September 2024 annexation of about 245 acres, alleging the Shaw Cemetery parcel's owner did not consent as required by KRS 81A.412(1).

The Joint City-County Planning Commission filed its response in the moratorium suit, stating no development plan accompanied the application and that it would take no further action until the litigation concludes.
Cave City residents held a protest against the proposed hyperscale data center near Mammoth Cave National Park.

Attorney Thomas Davis filed the Joint City-County Planning Commission's response to the annexation lawsuit, requesting dismissal with prejudice so the commission could decide applications under its rules and applicable state law.
A Barren County Circuit Court hearing was scheduled on Kentucky Industrial Alliance's request for a preliminary injunction to temporarily block enforcement of the moratorium.
A community town hall on the proposed data center was scheduled for July 21 at Austin Tracy Elementary School.

projects.name: Project Delta
projects.note: Hyperscale data center on 1,800 acres near Dan River; 998 acres developable, rest is floodplain. Originally approved by commissioners Jan 2026 but rescinded in April after a lawsuit (SCSJ/SELC) challenged the public hearing notice. ELS reapplied in late July 2026. Planning board voted 5-2 to recommend denial on Aug 14, 2026. Commissioners make the final decision. Closed-loop cooling and possible on-site generation planned.

events.summary: Project Delta hyperscale data center proposed near Walnut Cove.
The Stokes County planning board recommended denial of the Project Delta rezoning for the first time, in December 2025, before commissioners later approved it anyway.
Stokes County commissioners approve rezoning despite planning board denial and public opposition.
Community groups and residents file lawsuit challenging the rezoning (SCSJ/SELC).
Commissioners vote to rescind January rezoning approval after lawsuit revealed notice violations.
Engineered Land Solutions held a community information session on Project Delta on June 4, 2026, according to the Southern Coalition for Social Justice.
Engineered Land Solutions held a second community information session on Project Delta on July 8, 2026, per the Southern Coalition for Social Justice.
The Stokes County planning board voted 6-1 to recommend a six-month moratorium on data center development to give the county time to study impacts.
Stokes County commissioners voted 3-2 to reject the planning board's recommended six-month data center moratorium and approved text amendments regulating data centers in the county.
ELS submits new conditional use application for Project Delta.
Planning board votes 5-2 to recommend denial of Project Delta conditional use application.
Stokes County commissioners are scheduled to hold a public hearing on September 8, 2026 to make the final decision on the Project Delta rezoning.

projects.name: Smithfield Gateway Data Center
projects.operator: DEPG Mosier Associates LP / DEPG of Shawnee II LP
projects.note: Two 250,000 sq ft data center buildings proposed at Smithfield Gateway behind St. Luke's and Wawa on Route 209. Developer filed a curative amendment application; township initiated a 180-day review period starting May 6, 2026. Township is proposing a new H-1 (Heavy Industrial) Zoning District where data centers would be the only permitted conditional use, removing them from ED and M-1 districts. Board of Supervisors held public hearing and vote on Aug 12, 2026.

events.summary: The township held a public hearing on its data center ordinance on October 22, 2025, and the ordinance passed.
In November 2025 DEPG submitted the initial sketch plan application and supporting documents for the Smithfield Gateway data center (Phases 1B, 2A, and 2B).
In December 2025 the Township Engineer issued Sketch Plan Review No. 1 after the applicant submitted a conceptual site plan, grading plans, and cross-section plans.
The applicant resubmitted revised sketch plan materials, including revised conceptual plans, preliminary renderings, a sound study, and response letters to the Township Engineer.
The Township Engineer issued Sketch Plan Review No. 2 for the Smithfield Gateway data center sketch plan.

A Change.org petition titled 'Stop the massive data center in Stroudsburg, PA' opposing the Smithfield Gateway Project was launched, citing energy use, deforestation, noise and light pollution, and questioning promised job benefits.

DataCenterDynamics reported the Smithfield Gateway project, discussed by the Planning Commission in mid-February, would consist of two 250,000 sq ft data centers linked to Legend Properties with no disclosed end-user, and that an opposition petition had passed 800 signatures.

DEPG Mosier Associates LP and DEPG of Shawnee II LP submitted the conditional use application for a two-building data center at Smithfield Gateway, including a statement of purpose, conditional use plan, environmental impact summary, traffic statement, and sound emissions study.
The township scheduled an April 22, 2026 6:00 p.m. hearing on a data center ordinance amendment.
Curative amendment application filed; 180-day MPC review period begins.
In June 2026 the Township Engineer (T&M Associates) issued Review No. 1 on the data center conditional use application.
The township scheduled a Board of Supervisors meeting for June 3, 2026 at 6:00 p.m. at J.T. Lambert Intermediate School to discuss data center ordinance updates.

The applicant resubmitted the conditional use application with revised documents, including conditional use plans, a Kaplin-Stewart resubmission letter, traffic memorandum, acoustical evaluation, emergency response plan, detailed load study report, and water and sewer letters.
Board of Supervisors public hearing and curative amendment vote at JT Lambert Intermediate School.

Fox56 covered the public hearing at J.T. Lambert Intermediate School where residents voiced opposition to the proposed data center zoning, quoting resident Joel Raffaeli saying the community could come up with something better.

Township newsletter states the Planning Commission will review the conditional use application for the proposed data center and vote on a recommendation to the Board of Supervisors on Thursday, August 13 at 7:00 p.m.

Township newsletter announces the Board of Supervisors will open the conditional use hearing on the proposed data center on Wednesday, September 9 at 6:00 p.m. at J.T. Lambert Intermediate School, where party status requests are due.

projects.name: Energence Utah Digital Infrastructure Campus
projects.note: Massive 5,046-acre multi-use campus with 475-acre data center area (expandable to 1,000+ acres), 200-acre energy center, and ~1,440 acres of solar. Targets 100 MW by Year 2, 700 MW by Year 4, up to 1.2 GW firm / 1.9 GW total by Year 6. Senmiao Technology (NASDAQ: AIHS) entered a non-binding LOI for $5M staged investment for 51% equity in Energence Utah. Campus already has active conditional-use permits and 100,000 MMBTU/day gas commitment. Very early stage (LOI, not binding) and highly speculative given micro-cap sponsor.

events.summary: Utah Inland Port Authority Board officially adopted the 2,780-acre Black Gold Project Area in Duchesne County and Roosevelt City, creating an economic development zone that the Energence Utah campus would later cite as its location.
Senmiao Technology enters LOI for $5M investment for 51% stake in Energence Utah; 100 MW targeted in initial 2-year phase.

Pulse 2.0 reported additional details from the LOI: the 5,046-acre campus already holds active conditional-use permits for the data campus, gas generation, energy storage, and solar PV, and has secured an initial natural gas commitment of 100,000 MMBTU per day, with Elio Energy Group serving as the development services provider.

Senmiao Technology filed its 10-Q with the SEC disclosing that starting in 2026 the company began evaluating expansion into AI infrastructure, appointed David Nichols as strategic advisor for power infrastructure and capital formation, and in July 2026 formed Nebula Matrix AI LLC (90% owned) with Constant Energy Construction Corp. to develop AI data centers in the U.S.

projects.name: Andover HPC Data Center
projects.note: National Land Developers registered Andover HPC Development in December 2025 at 248 Stickles Pond Road, a 97-acre former airport site. Andover Township first allowed data centers in a redevelopment zone along Route 206 (September 2025) and raised the height limit to 65 feet (April 2026), but after a chaotic May 2026 meeting with 300 residents, the township passed Ordinance 2026-13 banning data centers township-wide. No formal site plan was ever filed. National Land Developers sued in Sussex County Superior Court on July 10, 2026, challenging the ban.
