events.summary: In September 2021 the Township Committee adopted Resolution 2021-91, designating approximately 812 acres along the Route 206 corridor (43 tax lots, including the Stickles Pond Road parcel) as a Non-Condemnation Area in Need of Redevelopment.
In 2024 the 97-acre property at 248 Stickles Pond Road received approval for a 660,000-square-foot warehouse development with little public opposition.
In August 2025 township officials first publicly discussed a potential data center at a committee meeting.
Township passes ordinance allowing data centers in Route 206 redevelopment zone.
Approximately 33 days after the September 2025 ordinance permitting data centers, the property owner satisfied a $1.28 million mortgage on the Stickles Pond Road parcel.
Andover HPC Development LLC registered at 248 Stickles Pond Road address.
Township committee votes to raise height limit to 65 feet in redevelopment zone.

Attorney Anand Dash, representing community group Andover Responsible Development (a fiscally sponsored member of the NJ Highlands Coalition), filed a legal notice challenging Ordinances 2025-15 and 2026-08 as violations of state Municipal Land Use Law, threatening suit if they were not rescinded by May 7.
Chaotic meeting with ~300 residents opposing data center; police confrontation.

At the same contentious meeting, the Township Committee voted 4-1 to introduce an ordinance creating additional data center standards including closed-loop water cooling, noise controls, and electric substation requirements; five days later they reversed course and introduced a ban instead.

NJTODAY reported that the township attorney confirmed preliminary PILOT financial discussions had taken place behind closed doors, and identified recently formed entities Bridge AIX LLC and Bridge AI Group LLC linked to the project through Delaware registrations.
Mayor Tom Walsh posted a video statement saying the Township Committee had directed the township attorney to draft an ordinance repealing data centers as a permitted use.
At a special meeting the Township Committee introduced Ordinance 2026-13, a township-wide data center ban that would repeal the two prior ordinances permitting them.
The Andover Township Land Use Board found Ordinance 2026-13 consistent with the township's master plan.
The Township Committee unanimously adopted Ordinance 2026-13, prohibiting data centers as a use in all zones townshipwide.
National Land Developers files lawsuit in Sussex County Superior Court challenging Ordinance 2026-13 banning data centers.
Andover officials said they intend to vigorously defend the ordinance, have no interest in settling, and expect to file a response to the complaint within about 30 days.
The Sussex County Democratic Committee issued a written statement criticizing township officials over the ordinance's vulnerability to the developer's lawsuit.

Insider NJ reported Mayor Walsh stated the township has funding in place to defend the ordinance; Sussex County Republican chair Joseph LaBarbera denied Democratic allegations that the GOP was lobbying for data centers, calling the claim a deliberate lie.

projects.name: Pennhurst Data Center Campus
projects.note: Penn Hurst Holdings proposed a 1.9 million-square-foot data center campus on 123 acres of the historic Pennhurst State School and Hospital site. The East Vincent Township Board of Supervisors voted unanimously to deny the conditional use application on May 21, 2026. Penn Hurst Holdings appealed to Chester County Court of Common Pleas on June 26, arguing irreconcilable contradictions in the township's zoning code.

events.summary: East Vincent Board of Supervisors unanimously denies conditional use application for 1.9M sq ft data center.
Township issues written denial decision.
Penn Hurst Holdings files appeal to Chester County Court of Common Pleas.

projects.name: Karis Critical Plum Farms Data Center
projects.note: Karis Critical acquired 180 acres known as Plum Farms at the northwest corner of Route 59 and Higgins Road for $45 million and sought rezoning for a data center. The village planning commission gave a negative recommendation in early June 2026. After weeks of community backlash, Karis notified the village on July 1 that it would withdraw the rezoning request. Governor Pritzker had also suspended state data center incentives. Karis has not indicated whether it will refile.

events.summary: Village planning commission votes against rezoning recommendation.
Karis Critical withdraws rezoning request after community opposition.

projects.name: Site Layer 4 Data Center Campus
projects.note: Site Layer 4, a New York-based firm, has applied to rezone 5,344 acres of ranchland on the Lazy V Six Ranch northeast of Wheatland for a $26 billion data center campus with co-located utility-scale energy generation. The project promises 300 jobs and substantial tax revenue but neighbors are concerned about water, wildlife, and viewshed impacts. More than 400 public comments were received. Planning and Zoning Commission hearing rescheduled to August 26, 2026, with County Commissioners hearing on September 2.

events.summary: Rezoning application revealed for 5,344-acre data center campus on Lazy V Six Ranch.
Planning and Zoning Commission public hearing at Agriplex, Wheatland.
Platte County Commissioners public hearing at Agriplex, Wheatland.

projects.name: Project Bluestem
projects.note: Cloverleaf Infrastructure proposes Project Bluestem, a 600 MW hyperscale data center on approximately 1,000 acres of former Tailgate Ranch land south of Tonganoxie. The Leavenworth County Commission passed a 90-day moratorium on data center applications in May 2026, which expired in August. On August 5, commissioners voted 3-2 against extending the moratorium. On August 13, officials reversed course and directed planning and zoning to delay regulation recommendations until after a joint work session before the September meeting. No formal application has been submitted.

events.summary: Leavenworth County residents pack public forum on proposed data center.

Coverage identified Cloverleaf Infrastructure as the developer of Project Bluestem, a conceptual 1,000-acre data center near Tonganoxie that could require up to 1.2 gigawatts of power and would receive a 100% sales and use tax abatement for 20 years, with no formal applications yet submitted.

The opposition group Citizens Against Bluestem held its inaugural meeting at the Tonganoxie VFW Post Home, drawing roughly 150 attendees; speakers included County Commissioner Mike Stieben and a Sierra Club representative.
Leavenworth County Commission passes 90-day moratorium on data center applications.
The Tongie Data Center Watch Dog Group planned to present a petition to the Tonganoxie City Council at 7 p.m. on Monday, May 19, seeking an 18-month moratorium on data center development.
Project Bluestem representatives held an open house at 304 Venue in Tonganoxie to address resident concerns about the proposed data center.
Commission votes 3-2 against extending moratorium; moratorium expires.
Officials reverse course, direct P&Z to delay recommendations until joint work session in September.
About 100 protesters organized by the Tongie Data Center WatchDog Group packed the Leavenworth County planning meeting, where the planning commission voted 8-1 to revisit data center regulations.

projects.name: Muncy Township Data Center
projects.note: DANKO Holdings II / Fishlips LLC filed a zoning permit application on April 15, 2026, and a conditional use application on April 28, for three data center buildings along John Brady Drive near Yetter Road, about two miles east of the closed Lycoming Mall. The township failed to hold the required hearing within 60 days, and the developer published a legal notice in July claiming 'deemed approval' under the state Municipalities Planning Code. Supervisors imposed a nine-month moratorium on data center submissions in June 2026. The legal status of the deemed-approval claim is unresolved.

events.summary: Zoning permit application filed by DANKO Holdings II / Fishlips LLC.
Conditional use application filed for three data center buildings.
Township supervisors impose nine-month moratorium on data center submissions.
Developer publishes legal notice claiming deemed approval due to township's failure to hold hearing within 60 days.

projects.name: Urbana Technology Hub
projects.note: Thor Equities assembled approximately 230 acres near Ohio 55 and US 68 for a 460,000 sq ft, $1B+ data center campus called the Urbana Technology Hub. A site plan application was submitted February 13 but deemed incomplete by city staff. The BZA unanimously denied Thor's appeal. The city council then adopted new zoning codes removing data centers as a permitted use in the M-1 manufacturing district. Thor Equities filed a federal lawsuit in the US District Court for the Southern District of Ohio. A charter amendment petition and mayor recall effort are also underway.

events.summary: Urbana City Council approved a zoning code modification permitting data centers in the M-1 Light Manufacturing District and annexed Thor Equities' property.
Urbana Owner I LLC (linked to Thor Equities) purchased a 47.6-acre parcel near the proposed site for $2,143,665.
In November 2025, city council approved a Community Reinvestment Area (CRA2) tax abatement agreement for the data center site after three readings.
Highland55 Investments LLC purchased 85.6 acres southwest of Urbana for $3,210,712.50, the second major land assembly for the campus.
City Director of Administration Spencer Mitchell publicly confirmed for the first time that a property owner had approached the city about developing a data center.
Council members discussed data center concerns at a regular meeting and directed Law Director Feinstein to prepare moratorium legislation for the February 17 meeting.
Site plan application submitted by Choice One Engineering on behalf of Thor Equities; deemed incomplete by city staff.
City council voted 5-2 to remove a proposed 12-month data center moratorium from the agenda; approximately 50 residents attended the meeting.
Data center plans revealed at city meeting.
Thor Equities issued a public statement on the proposed data center, describing it as a $1 billion private investment and pledging water conservation, stable electric rates, and community investment.
Urbana City Council passed a 12-month moratorium on new data centers by a 6-1 vote, with Audra Bean the sole dissenter; about 40 residents spoke afterward mostly in support.

Ideastream reported the moratorium left the $1 billion proposal in limbo and identified CyrusOne as a project partner alongside Thor Equities; an online petition opposing the project had gathered over 4,000 signatures within two weeks.
Thor Equities formally appeals city's determination that application was incomplete.
BZA unanimously denies Thor's appeal, upholding city determination that site plan application was incomplete.
Thor Equities launched a project information website, urbanaohiodatacenter.com, with a project overview, economic-benefit claims, and a contact form.

Thor Equities publicized economic-impact figures for the project: over $1 billion investment, more than $5.8 million in annual local tax revenue, over 1,000 construction jobs, and 30 to 80 permanent positions.
City council adopts new zoning codes removing data centers as permitted use in M-1 district.
Thor Equities purchased approximately 97 acres from Organ Farms LLC for about $3.4 million, adding a southern access point from U.S. Highway 68 to the proposed campus.
A public hearing was held on the proposed ordinance to reverse the 2025 zoning amendment and remove data centers as a permitted use in the M-1 district.
City council unanimously passed Ordinance 4635-26, restoring the pre-2025 zoning code and completing the removal of data centers as a permitted M-1 use; residents applauded the vote.
Thor Equities files federal lawsuit against City of Urbana in US District Court, Southern District of Ohio.

In July 2026, Thor Equities launched a direct mail, television, and digital advertising campaign aimed at Urbana residents, describing it as an educational effort to counter misinformation about the project.

Two Urbana residents launched petitions: Nicole Nawman began a charter-amendment petition to bar hyperscale data centers, and James Cropper began a petition to recall Mayor Bill Bean over alleged lack of transparency.
City Law Director Mark Feinstein submitted his resignation to Mayor Bean, effective August 7, 2026, citing a new legal opportunity and family priorities; the city began recruiting a replacement.
Nicole Nawman turned in the charter-amendment petition packet to the Champaign County Board of Elections, saying signatures well surpassed the required minimum.
The Champaign County Board of Elections reported the mayoral recall petitions collected enough valid signatures for the recall question to appear on the November 3 general election ballot.

A Champaign County Common Pleas judge ordered the city to provide a complete transcript of the April 13 BZA hearing and set briefing deadlines through October 2026; the ruling did not decide the merits of the case.

Urbana City Council approved emergency Ordinance No. 4640-26, sending the proposed data-center-ban charter amendment to the November 3, 2026 ballot, suspending rules to meet the August 5 filing deadline.

Three candidates filed petitions by the August 5 deadline to replace Mayor Bean if he is recalled; Eugene Fields Jr. and Nicole Nawman met the 169-signature threshold while Taylor Armstrong fell four signatures short.

The Champaign County Board of Elections forwarded the charter-amendment petition to the Ohio Secretary of State after finding a typographical error referencing Article VII instead of Article VIII, leaving its ballot status uncertain.

projects.name: Colossus 2
projects.note: Chip types: B200,B300. Epoch AI estimates ~946 MW.

events.summary: xAI announced it had begun installing computing infrastructure at its expanded Southwest Memphis data center on Tulane Road, called Colossus 2, saying 110,000 Nvidia GB200 GPUs were being installed.
Earthjustice and the Southern Environmental Law Center announced they had sent xAI a 60-day Clean Air Act notice of intent to sue over unpermitted gas turbines in Southaven powering Colossus 2.

A Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality public hearing in Southaven on xAI's permit for 41 permanent gas turbines drew hundreds of attendees and, per the report, unanimous opposition from residents citing noise and air-pollution concerns.

The Mississippi Environmental Quality Permit Board unanimously granted xAI affiliate MZX Tech an air permit to install 41 methane gas-fired turbines at its Southaven facility, over community opposition.

The Mississippi State Conference of the NAACP and the national NAACP, represented by SELC and Earthjustice, filed suit against xAI and its subsidiary MZX Tech in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Mississippi, alleging illegal operation of unpermitted gas turbines under the Clean Air Act.

The NAACP filed a request for a preliminary injunction asking the court to immediately halt xAI's unpermitted air pollution from what it called an illegal power plant, then powering Colossus 2 with 33 unpermitted gas turbines.

The U.S. Department of Justice moved to intervene in the NAACP lawsuit and asked the court to dismiss it, arguing that shutting off power to the Colossus 2 data center would harm national security because xAI's Grok supports Department of Defense military operations.

Records obtained via public-records request (Trinity Consultants emails to Mississippi regulators) revealed xAI had operated 59 unpermitted gas turbines for Colossus 2, roughly double the 27 the company had publicly acknowledged in January, with at least 57 sited in Southaven, Mississippi.

The Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality issued an agreed order setting a retirement schedule for xAI's 69 temporary trailer-mounted turbines at the Southaven site, requiring decommissioning to begin August 18, 2026, with most units retired by April 2027 and the most recently added by July 14, 2027, after supply-chain delays to the 41 permanent turbines.

projects.name: Microsoft Fairwater Atlanta
projects.note: Part of Microsoft AI WAN. Chip types: B200. Epoch AI estimates ~636 MW.

events.summary: Fayetteville City Council voted 5-0 to annex and rezone 412 acres from R-70 residential to Business Park for a data center office park, with 18 rezoning conditions attached; approximately 24 residents spoke in opposition, some in tears.

QTS purchased 615 acres in Fayetteville for $153.8 million (approximately $250,000 per acre) from the Fayette County Development Authority, brokered by CBRE, for what it called the world's largest multi-tenant data center campus.

QTS publicly announced Project Excalibur: a planned 6.6 million sq ft campus of 16 data center buildings plus 400,000 sq ft of office space on the 615-acre Fayetteville site, with construction to start in 2023 and full build-out by 2032, investing over $1 billion.

Fayetteville Planning and Zoning Commission approved the conceptual site plan and schematic building elevations for the Excalibur Data Center after a 5-6 month Development of Regional Impact review involving GDOT and the Georgia Department of Community Affairs.
Land clearing began at the QTS Project Excalibur site in April 2023, per Epoch AI satellite imagery analysis.

Fayetteville City Council unanimously approved a development agreement between the City and National Acquisition Company, LLC (QTS affiliate) for the 612-acre data center campus at 1435 Highway 54 West.

The Fayette County Development Authority proposed 'Project Rita,' a 96 MW data center campus on 145.5 acres in Tyrone (adjacent to the QTS site), comprising two buildings totaling 490,000 sq ft with a requested Business Technology Park rezoning; the Town Council hearing was scheduled for March 21.

Tyrone Town Council approved the rezoning for the Microsoft data center (Project Rita) on approximately 147 acres on North Highway 74, following Planning Commission and Town Council public hearings on February 22 and March 21 respectively.
The first building on the QTS campus received its certificate of occupancy in May 2025, per the AJC, with a construction completion certificate issued September 25, 2025.

Fayette County Water System sent a letter to QTS revealing that a water meter installed during a system-wide smart-meter upgrade had not been read electronically, resulting in approximately 13 million gallons of unrecorded usage and a retroactive bill of approximately $147,000; the issue was discovered after a neighbor reported low water pressure.
Microsoft's Fairwater 2 data center on the QTS campus began operations in October 2025, spanning more than 1 million sq ft and using closed-loop cooling described as consuming almost zero water.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella announced the Fayetteville facility as part of the world's first AI superfactory, connecting the Atlanta Fairwater 2 site with Fairwater 1 in Wisconsin across a single flat network to train AI models at planet scale.

In January 2026 Fayetteville City Council passed a 90-day moratorium on new data center development applications while working to revise the Unified Development Ordinance; City Manager Ray Gibson stated 'we do not want anymore data centers in our community.'

WBRC reported on community impacts from the QTS/Microsoft campus, with resident Diana Dietz citing heavy truck traffic on residential roads, transmission lines through neighborhoods, and concerns over rising power and water bills; QTS stated it uses water-free cooling and is committed to paying its fair share of power costs.

Crow Holdings Development withdrew its appeal of a denied data center project on Highway 85 North in Fayetteville one day before the scheduled City Council hearing; the city had also enacted UDO changes on March 5 that made data centers no longer permissible.

QTS Fayetteville I DC1-2, LLC began sounding out investors for $5.4 billion in new debt ($4.9 billion secured bond plus $500 million term loan) to finance expansion of the Fayetteville campus leased to Microsoft, under an updated green bond framework with a PUE threshold tightened from 1.5 to 1.4.

projects.name: Anthropic-Amazon New Carlisle
projects.note: Part of Project Rainier. Chip types: Trainium2. Epoch AI estimates ~910 MW.

events.summary: St. Joseph County Redevelopment Commission approved Resolution 2023-16, a development facilitation agreement between the Commission, the Indiana Economic Development Corporation, and Razor5 LLC for pre-development activities on 640 acres in the New Carlisle Economic Development Area.

Local media reported construction activity already underway on the Razor5 site near New Carlisle, including an electrical substation pad on 45 acres near Edison Road and excavation on the northern parcel, before the developer's identity was publicly confirmed.

St. Joseph County Area Plan Commission voted 6-1 to give a favorable recommendation for rezoning over 800 acres at 31000 State Road 2 from agricultural to industrial classification for the Razor5 project, sparking complaints from New Carlisle residents.

St. Joseph County Council voted 8-1 to rezone approximately 640 acres of agricultural land near New Carlisle to industrial use for the Razor5 LLC project, with Council Republican Joe Thomas casting the lone dissenting vote.

Tax abatement proposal documents presented to the St. Joseph County Council revealed the Razor5 project would total $11 billion in investment across 640 acres and a secondary 280-acre parcel, projecting 400 full-time jobs at approximately $30 per hour.

Governor Eric Holcomb announced Amazon Web Services plans to invest $11 billion to build a data center campus near New Carlisle, the largest capital investment in Indiana history, with at least 1,000 jobs over 10 years; state incentives included up to $18.3 million in tax credits, $55 million in Hoosier Business Investment credits, and $7 million for State Road 2 improvements.

St. Joseph County Council committee voted a favorable recommendation on the Amazon data center tax abatement declaratory resolution, advancing it to the full county council for a public hearing scheduled for June 11.

St. Joseph County Council voted 7-2 to approve the Amazon data center incentive package: a 10-year 50% real property tax abatement on 870 acres, an 85% enterprise technology exemption on personal property for 35 years, and a community enhancement agreement valued at approximately $143 million.

Amazon held a ceremonial groundbreaking for Project Rainier at Century Center in South Bend, attended by Governor Holcomb and AWS VP Kevin Miller; construction on the 870-acre site had already been underway for months prior to the ceremony.

In September 2025, the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission unanimously approved the creation of NIPSCO Generation LLC (GenCo), described as America's first data center-only utility subsidiary, to generate and sell electricity exclusively to hyperscale data centers including the Amazon New Carlisle campus.

Amazon announced Project Rainier was operational in New Carlisle with seven data center buildings running approximately 500,000 Trainium2 chips dedicated to training Anthropic's Claude AI models, making it the largest known deployment of non-Nvidia compute in the world.

Amazon announced an additional $15 billion investment in new data center campuses across northern Indiana, bringing total committed investment to approximately $26 billion, with a NIPSCO energy deal projected to save existing ratepayers $1 billion over 15 years.

NIPSCO filed plans to supply up to 3 GW to Amazon data centers in northern Indiana through GenCo, which will build two 1.3-GW gas-fired power plants and a 400-MW battery storage system, with power deliveries beginning January 1, 2027, and ramping to 2.4 GW by end of 2032.

Four Republican members of the St. Joseph County Council sent Amazon a letter asking it to renegotiate its 35-year property tax abatement, citing Microsoft's national policy of forgoing local tax breaks and the region's inherent advantages including one of the nation's richest aquifers.

Amazon granted local media the first look at the New Carlisle data center campus administration building and workforce development programs; the first work-based learning cohort of 58 local graduates had completed training in machine learning and data center operations.

AWS announced its New Carlisle campus investment had reached $13.8 billion with 18 of approximately 30 planned buildings operational, over 1,000 employees hired (approximately 450 from St. Joseph County), and up to 4,000 construction workers on site during peak phases.

projects.name: Meta Prometheus
projects.note: Part of Prometheus. Chip types: B200. Epoch AI estimates ~562 MW.

events.summary: Meta announced a further expansion of its New Albany data center campus, adding buildings that brought total investment in Ohio to more than $1.5 billion and supporting 300 operational jobs and 1,200 peak construction workers.

Power Engineering reported that Will-Power (Williams Companies) had filed with the Ohio Power Siting Board for two behind-the-meter natural gas plants, Socrates North and Socrates South, each 200 MW, at Meta's New Albany International Business Park campus, with a planned in-service date of Q3 2026.

The Ohio Power Siting Board approved the Socrates South Power Generation Project, a 200 MW behind-the-meter natural gas plant in Licking County to be built by Will-Power OH (a Williams Companies subsidiary) to serve exclusively Sidecat, part of Meta Platforms, on its 740-acre New Albany Business Park campus.

Power Engineering reported that construction on the Socrates South 200 MW natural gas plant serving Sidecat (Meta) in New Albany was planned to begin in June 2025 with expected completion in November 2026, detailing the turbine fleet including Solar Turbines Titan 250s, Siemens SGT400s, and Caterpillar reciprocating engines.

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg announced on Threads and Facebook that Meta's first AI supercluster, Prometheus, a 1-gigawatt data center in New Albany, Ohio, will come online in 2026, alongside a larger Hyperion cluster and hundreds of billions of dollars in compute investment.

A Meta engineering blog post described Prometheus as a 1-gigawatt cluster spanning multiple traditional data center buildings plus weatherproof tents and adjacent colocation facilities, and said the buildout was currently underway.

In early November 2025, Turner Construction evacuated over 1,000 workers from the Prometheus data center construction site in New Albany after a terminated contractor returned and threatened a supervisor with a firearm; security confiscated the weapon and law enforcement responded.

Spectrum News 1 reported on Meta's Prometheus in New Albany as potentially the world's first gigawatt-scale data center, noting on-site gas-fired power plants; Mayor Sloan Spalding said the facility would not draw energy off the grid, and residents raised concerns about local power reliability.

Meta announced nuclear energy agreements with Oklo, Vistra and TerraPower for up to 6.6 GW by 2035, stating the projects will deliver power to grids supporting its operations including the Prometheus supercluster in New Albany, Ohio.

WOSU reported that a University of Virginia/Joyce Foundation study found Columbus will become the second-largest data center hub in the Great Lakes region behind Chicago, noting Meta is wrapping up construction on its Prometheus gigawatt-scale data center in New Albany and that Ohio data centers currently consume 5.3% of the state's energy, projected to reach 10.9% within four years.

events.summary: Indiana Governor Eric Holcomb announced Meta will build an $800 million, roughly 700,000-square-foot data center campus at River Ridge Commerce Center in Jeffersonville, Meta's 18th U.S. and 22nd global data center.
Construction on the Jeffersonville facility was set to begin that month and be complete in 2026, supporting more than 1,250 construction jobs and 100 permanent tech jobs.

Community groups including Hoosier Action and Clark County Moms held a meeting to organize opposition to the Meta data center, citing concerns the facility could use up to 5 million gallons of water daily and raise local utility costs.

Meta said it had contributed nearly $500,000 to schools and nonprofits since its 2024 groundbreaking and announced a new Community Action Grants program for Clark County, amid community concerns over a Duke Energy 11% residential rate increase set to take effect in early 2026.

The Jeffersonville City Council unanimously passed a one-year moratorium on new data center development (suspending normal rules to push it through three readings in one session), but the Meta facility already under construction at River Ridge is exempt due to federal/state control of the former Indiana Army Ammunition Plant site.

The city disclosed that Meta paid $4 million upfront in wastewater capacity fees and is projected to generate $300,000-$400,000 in monthly recurring sewer utility revenue once the facility is operational.

events.summary: The Oregonian reporter Mike Rogoway submitted a public records request to the City of The Dalles for records of Google's local water usage, which the city denied by claiming the data was a trade secret, triggering the ensuing legal fight (September 2021).
The Dalles city council authorized an infrastructure agreement with Google (via subsidiary Design LLC) worth $28.5 million for water system improvements.

Google signed a Strategic Investment Program agreement with The Dalles providing property tax breaks in exchange for the company's investment commitments, alongside a $28.5 million infrastructure agreement.

The Dalles settled its lawsuit against The Oregonian, agreeing to release ten years of Google water-usage records to reporter Mike Rogoway and to have Google reimburse the city's $53,173 in legal fees to the newspaper.

The Dalles' community development department gave Whiting-Turner Contracting Co. approval to begin construction on a 290,000-square-foot, roughly $600 million Google data center building for Google subsidiary Design LLC at the former aluminum smelter site.
Google completed construction of a fourth data center building at its The Dalles campus in 2025.

H.R. 655, the Dalles Watershed Development Act sponsored by Rep. Cliff Bentz, which would transfer about 150 acres of Mt. Hood National Forest land to The Dalles to expand its reservoir, passed the U.S. House and moved to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee.

OPB reported that Google's water consumption in The Dalles rose 316% from 2012 to 2024 (from 104 million to 434 million gallons annually) while the city's population grew only 12%, and that a bill (H.R. 655) would transfer Mount Hood National Forest land to the city to expand its reservoir.

The Dalles Mayor Richard Mays publicly called OPB's reporting on Google's data center water use inaccurate; OPB's follow-up corrected one error, noting projected residential water rate increases by 2036 were 99%, not the 7% initially reported.

A coalition of 13 organizations including WaterWatch of Oregon, Bark, Columbia Riverkeeper, Sierra Club, and Oregon Wild sent a letter pressuring Senator Wyden to oppose H.R. 655, stating Google has received about $260 million in state and local tax breaks at its The Dalles campus.

Construction began in late January 2026 on Google's Building 5 at the Midlothian campus, with an estimated completion date of February 2027.

Meta awarded Hensel Phelps the $800 million Kuna data center project (preconstruction and construction services), with groundbreaking scheduled for September 2022 and construction expected to continue through 2025.
The Kuna City Council formally approved the Urban Renewal Plan for the Kuna East Urban Renewal Project via Ordinance No. 2022-34, establishing the district around the Meta project site.

Construction Review Online reports Meta restarted work at Temple and Kuna after halting globally to redesign data centers for denser GPU installations for AI applications.

Construction Dive reports JE Dunn resumed construction on Meta's Temple data center after the December 2022 pause; Meta says the AI-optimized redesign is 31% less expensive and takes half the time to build; completion shifted from 2025 to 2026.

GovTech reports Minnesota-based Oppidan Investment Co. purchased 10 acres from the Temple Economic Development Corp. in March 2025 and plans a $31 million, 61,554-square-foot data center at 2325 Eberhardt Road directly across from Meta's campus.

Meta officially opens its $1.2 billion AI-optimized data center on Industrial Boulevard in Temple; the 760,000-square-foot, two-building campus supports nearly 100 operations jobs and employed over 1,200 trade workers at peak construction.

projects.name: Meta Cheyenne

events.summary: The Cheyenne Public Services Committee approved a development agreement for 'Project Cosmo,' a data center development by Goat Systems LLC on 945 acres in the High Plains Business Park.

Meta formally announced its Cheyenne data center: an $800 million, 715,000-square-foot campus at High Plains Business Park expected to support about 100 jobs, with over 1,000 construction workers at peak and a 2027 online target, built by Fortis Construction with Black Hills Energy supplying grid resources.

Cheyenne City Council voted 8-1 against a proposed 12-month moratorium on new data center development, after nearly four hours of public comment citing water supply, noise, farmland conversion, and pace-of-change concerns.
The Cheyenne Board of Public Utilities discovered white bacterial colonies during routine wastewater system testing, later traced to Meta's Cheyenne Data Center contractor.
The Wyoming Public Health Laboratory identified the bacteria found in Cheyenne's reclaimed water system as Cupriavidus gilardii, an unusual soil bacterium.

Investigators confirmed the same bacteria was present at Meta's predischarge storage tank, and Cheyenne's Board of Public Utilities revoked Goat Systems LLC's industrial discharge permit for the Meta data center.

The Cheyenne Board of Public Utilities issued its first public statement on the contamination, about four months after the bacteria was first discovered, citing the Meta data center operator for 'serious noncompliance' with wastewater discharge standards and a $10,000 fine.

The Cheyenne Board of Public Utilities announced it would stop accepting industrial wastewater from data-center fill-and-flush and closed-loop cooling operations citywide following the Meta contamination incident.

Meta/Goat Systems filed a six-page appeal disputing the source of the bacteria contamination, asking the Cheyenne Board of Public Utilities for a contested-case hearing and a refund of the $10,000 fine.
