events.summary: The Vineland Planning Board approved Resolution 6652, authorizing NEP Real Estate of Vineland NJ Urban Renewal LLC to build 2,647,628 square feet of data centers in four phases over twelve years on the site off South Lincoln and Sheridan avenues.
Nebius announced a phased New Jersey data center expandable up to 300 MW total capacity, with first capacity expected as early as summer 2025 and 100 MW targeted by end of 2025.
The Vineland Planning Board approved Resolution 6720, amending the site plan to change the applicant to DataOne USA LLC and adding three power generation buildings to the campus.

Nebius signed a five-year GPU infrastructure supply deal with Microsoft worth $17.4 billion (up to $19.4 billion with added services), initially providing dedicated GPU capacity at its Vineland, New Jersey data center from later in 2025.
The Vineland City Council tabled a proposed UEZ revolving-fund loan for the DataOne project after significant public opposition at its December 9 meeting.
The Vineland City Council on December 23 approved a roughly $6.2 million ($6,198,786) Urban Enterprise Zone revolving-fund loan to help fund cranes for the DataOne construction project.
Residents packed a heated town hall at the Landis Theater in Vineland on January 21 to voice environmental concerns about the data center.

The Philadelphia Inquirer reported that South Jersey's largest data center was under construction in Vineland with completion expected November 2026, and that some residents said they had had no say in the process.
DataOne released an environmental impact statement for the Vineland data center facility, after phase-one construction was already underway and partially operational.

The Vineland City Council approved a resolution reducing public comment speaking time from five minutes to three minutes, after four months of longer-than-usual meetings driven by data center opposition.
The Cumberland County Department of Health inspected the DataOne site and issued a Notice of Violation for noise exceeding 50 decibels between 10 p.m. and 7 a.m.
About 100 residents rallied at Giampietro Memorial Park in Vineland against the data center; the event was organized by congressional candidate Bayly Winder and advocacy group Sustain SJ.
The Vineland Planning Board postponed a special meeting on DataOne's phase-two expansion (originally scheduled for March 26) to May 28, 2026, to give the company time to share plans with the public.

More than 60 environmental, labor, and community organizations signed a letter to Governor Sherrill calling for a moratorium on new data centers consuming at least 20 MW of electricity, citing Vineland among their concerns.

Residents Scott Montgomery and Michael Gentile filed a class-action lawsuit (Case 1:26-cv-05972) in U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey against DataOne USA LLC, alleging private nuisance, public nuisance, and negligence from continuous noise affecting approximately 1,013 households within one mile.

Governor Mikie Sherrill announced a four-pillar comprehensive plan to regulate data centers in New Jersey, including fair-share energy rules, transparency requirements, community benefit agreement standards, and prevailing wage mandates.
The Montgomery v. DataOne USA class-action lawsuit was voluntarily dismissed without prejudice after the court issued an order to show cause questioning subject-matter jurisdiction on June 12.

The Vineland Planning Board held a hearing at the Landis Theatre on DataOne's amended site plan for a phase-two expansion (adding a 587,980-square-foot building) to the 300 MW Nebius campus; opponent Helen Petrites presented 2,900 signatures and the board issued no decision that night.

A roughly six-hour Vineland Planning Board hearing on DataOne's proposed on-site fuel-cell power generation concluded around midnight on August 6 with no vote; the board said it would announce a date for a second hearing for further public comment.
NJBIA research analyst Jack Ramirez submitted written testimony to the Vineland Planning Board in support of the data center development.
The City of Vineland issued a stop-construction order for an LNG tank being installed at the DataOne site without prior approvals or permits.

The City of Vineland issued a second stop-construction order at the DataOne site, halting Bloom Energy fuel-cell installation work that was proceeding with no prior approvals, plans, or permits; violations carry $2,000 penalties per violation per day.
DA Davidson analyst Gil Luria cut the Nebius (NBIS) price target from $250 to $175, citing construction delays at the Vineland facility that he said may remove potential upside from 2026 guidance.

projects.name: Stream Phoenix
projects.note: Chip types: H100. Epoch AI estimates ~64 MW.

events.summary: Stream Data Centers announced its 157-acre Phoenix campus in Goodyear, AZ would open its first building in August 2020, with Cox Business as a key fiber provider and a 350 MW onsite APS substation.

Stream Data Centers commissioned Phoenix I, a 418,000 sq ft data center on its Goodyear campus, completing construction on schedule despite the pandemic, with power from an onsite Arizona Public Service (APS) substation.

Apollo Global Management announced it would acquire a majority stake in Stream Data Centers, with Phoenix listed among the company's key hyperscale campus markets; Goldman Sachs advised Stream on the deal.

Apollo-managed funds completed the acquisition of a majority interest in Stream Data Centers, with Principal Asset Management taking a minority stake; Stream's 4+ GW pipeline across U.S. markets including Phoenix transferred to the new ownership structure.

projects.name: Microsoft SAT14
projects.note: Chip types: H100,B300. Epoch AI estimates ~47 MW.

events.summary: Microsoft registered SAT14 Phase 1 (project TABS2021019142) with the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation for new construction of two building shells (152,000 sq ft and 107,000 sq ft) totaling 259,000 sq ft at 3545 Wiseman Boulevard, San Antonio, Bexar County, with an estimated cost of $154.9 million.
Construction began on SAT14 Phase 1 at 3545 Wiseman Boulevard, San Antonio, per the TDLR project filing; the design firm was Page Southerland Page of Austin.
SAT14 Phase 1 construction was completed and the TDLR project was closed, per the filing's recorded completion date.

Microsoft and EY published a June 2026 economic impact report for the San Antonio datacenter campus (Bexar and Medina Counties) showing $2.34 billion in construction economic activity since 2016, operations since 2019, 635 direct Microsoft jobs in 2025, $48.4 million in incremental tax revenue in Bexar and Medina Counties, and Microsoft as the number-one taxpayer in both counties.

Microsoft sent a letter to Governor Greg Abbott stating it has operated datacenters in Texas since 2016, hosts over 635 employees at its own facilities with 1,600-plus on-site contractors, and described its Community-First Infrastructure initiative and a behind-the-meter natural gas project in West Texas with Chevron.

projects.name: Vantage TX1
projects.note: Chip types: B200. Epoch AI estimates ~32 MW.

events.summary: Vantage Data Centers TX1 LLC filed TDLR architectural barriers project TABS2024007561 for 'Data Center Building TX11' at 14720 Omicron Dr, San Antonio — a 242,667 sq ft, 32 MW, two-story new-construction facility with estimated cost of $95.8 million and projected completion September 2026.
A transformer explosion near the Vantage Data Centers site in San Antonio injured one construction worker; SAPD and SAFD responded to the incident.

A TCEQ public hearing was held at a Marriott near SeaWorld regarding Vantage's air-quality permit for its Rogers Road (5207 Rogers Rd) facility; residents raised concerns about diesel generator emissions, noise, light pollution, and water usage. Vantage VP Michael Duplantis represented the company.

Deceleration.news reported that Vantage's two West Side San Antonio campuses (Omicron Drive and Rogers Road) were bringing major new pollution sources to the area, including on-site natural gas power plants and over 150 diesel backup generators.

San Antonio Current reported residents pushing back against the far West Side Vantage data center; the Rogers Road facility (360,000 sq ft, ~$157 million) was described as already constructed and partly operational, with 65 diesel backup generators and its own gas power plant.

Environmental Integrity Project, Sierra Club, and Public Citizen filed a notice of intent to sue Vantage and VoltaGrid under the Clean Air Act, alleging the Omicron Drive and Rogers Road campuses (combined 423 MW of generation, 151 diesel generators) improperly obtained minor-source permits to avoid major-source pollution controls; potential fines cited at up to $124,426 per day.

Texas Public Radio reported environmental groups threatening lawsuit over the two West Side Vantage campuses at 14270 Omicron Drive and 5207 Rogers Road; a TCEQ public hearing on Vantage's proposed federal operating permit for the Omicron Drive campus was scheduled for August 17, 2026.

WOAI/News4SA reported that Vantage obtained minor pollution source permits (typically for dry cleaners and gas stations) for its two San Antonio data center complexes, allowing it to bypass major-source pollution controls and community notification requirements.

projects.name: CoreWeave Dalton 1 & 2
projects.note: Chip types: B300. Epoch AI estimates ~28 MW.

events.summary: CoreWeave announced a definitive agreement to acquire Core Scientific in an all-stock transaction (implied equity value ~$9.0 billion), which would have given CoreWeave ownership of Core Scientific's ~1.3 GW gross power footprint, including its Georgia facilities.

Core Scientific shareholders voted against the proposed $9 billion CoreWeave merger (20.8M for, 203.5M against). The merger agreement was terminated with immediate effect; Core Scientific continues operating independently.

In its Q1 FY2026 earnings materials, Core Scientific stated that its Dalton, GA site has delivered Phase 1 (30 MW) with full completion targeted for early 2027, and that Dalton is one of five sites under its anchor hosting agreement with CoreWeave, with approximately 175 MW of contracted capacity.

Georgia EPD opened a public comment period on Application No. 29946, an air permit for Core Scientific's Dalton 01 facility at 2205 Industrial South Road covering 8 standby diesel generators with a combined maximum output of 21.6 MW.

projects.name: Google Pryor (North)
projects.note: Chip types: TPU v5p,TPU v5e. Epoch AI estimates ~53 MW.

events.summary: Google announced its initial data center investment in Mayes County, Oklahoma at MidAmerica Industrial Park, according to Google's own data center community page which lists 2007 as the year of first investment.
Google completed its first campus expansion at the Mayes County data center in 2012, per Google's official facility timeline.
Google completed a second expansion of the Mayes County data center campus in 2015, per Google's official facility timeline.
Google completed a third expansion of the Mayes County data center campus in 2019, per Google's official facility timeline.

Google announced a 9 exaflop cluster of Cloud TPU v4 pods in public preview at its Oklahoma data center, described as the world's largest publicly available ML hub, operating at 90% carbon-free energy with a PUE of 1.10.
A Google Cloud blog post confirmed that all Cloud TPU v4 supercomputers are housed at the Oklahoma data center, noting approximately 6x cleaner energy than typical on-premise data centers.

Epoch AI's data center tracker estimates Building 1 of Google Pryor (North) became operational around July 2024 with approximately 53 MW IT power, hosting an estimated 27,959 TPU v5p and 67,102 TPU v5e chips.

Epoch AI satellite imagery analysis shows Building 2 at Google Pryor (North) being retrofitted from a warehouse, with roof painting, cooling tower construction, and a new substation being built south of the building.

Google announced a $9 billion investment in Oklahoma cloud and AI infrastructure over two years, including expansion of the existing Pryor facility and a new data center campus in Stillwater, bringing total Oklahoma investment to $15 billion since 2007.

projects.name: xAI QTS Atlanta
projects.note: Chip types: H100,A100. Epoch AI estimates ~17 MW.

events.summary: Development Authority of Fulton County considered a $700,000,000 inducement and final bond resolution for X Corp. (f/k/a Twitter, Inc.) to acquire and install high-performance computing and AI infrastructure at 1025 Jefferson Street NW, Atlanta (QTS DC2), with the project described as competing with Portland and other locations.

Development Authority of Fulton County approved X Corp.'s $700M bond resolution 6-2 (Long and Lamont voting no), subject to a satisfactory corporate citizenship agreement, after X Corp. representatives confirmed the transaction covers equipment only and would retain 24 jobs plus 50 vendor employees.

Howell Station Neighborhood Association president Arthur Toal submitted to the DAFC board a Georgia Tech AI PhD candidate's analysis arguing X Corp.'s $700M equipment refit would not deliver the claimed economic benefits because the investment involves no new construction.

Core Scientific signs initial 200 MW, 12-year hosting contract with CoreWeave valued at over $3.5 billion in cumulative revenue; no specific sites named but this is the master contract the Muskogee facility later falls under.
Core Scientific announces a second 70 MW CoreWeave hosting agreement, bringing the total to 270 MW across two 12-year contracts worth approximately $4.7 billion in cumulative revenue.

CoreWeave exercises its final contract option for approximately 120 MW of additional critical IT load, bringing the total Core Scientific-CoreWeave commitment to approximately 500 MW across six sites with $8.7 billion in total potential revenue over 12 years.

Core Scientific and Port Muskogee break ground on a 100 MW HPC data center (70 MW for NVIDIA GPU computing load, 30 MW ancillary), part of the 500 MW CoreWeave contract; projected to generate $182 million in net local economic benefits, support 150 jobs, and bring over $12 million in property and sales taxes to local institutions; expected operational in 2026.

Core Scientific announces plans to expand its Muskogee campus to approximately 1.5 GW of gross power (1.0 GW leasable) through an agreement to acquire Polaris DS LLC and its 440 MW of grid-connected power under Oklahoma Gas & Electric service agreements, plus 250 acres secured for expansion; the first 70 MW building targets Q2 2026 delivery with NVIDIA GB300 platform, and a second 82.5 MW building targets Q4 2027.

Core Scientific completes acquisition of Polaris DS LLC for approximately $444 million in cash, securing roughly 440 MW of grid-connected power capacity under existing Oklahoma Gas & Electric service agreements to advance the planned 1.5 GW Muskogee campus expansion; next 82 MW building expected to reach customers in the second half of 2027.
Crusoe Energy Systems announced it is building a 200 MW data center at the Lancium Clean Campus outside Abilene, Texas.
Crusoe Energy Systems, Blue Owl Capital, and Primary Digital Infrastructure announced a $3.4 billion joint venture to fund and operate a 206 MW data center in Abilene, Texas.

Blackstone closed a $500 million equity investment in Lancium, whose first campus in Abilene is slated to come online in 2025; the Lancium project was originally announced in 2021 for cryptocurrency mining before pivoting to AI.

An SEC filing showed Crusoe Energy secured $686 million of a targeted $818 million raise from 70 investors; the Abilene campus is expected to be leased to Oracle, which will in turn rent it to Microsoft and OpenAI.

OpenAI, SoftBank, and Oracle announced the Stargate project at the White House, a venture to invest up to $500 billion in AI data center infrastructure including 10 data centers, with one already under construction in Texas.

OpenAI confirmed it was breaking ground on Stargate's first site in Abilene, with a requirement to create at least 57 full-time positions earning an average wage of $57,600 annually; OpenAI VP Chris Lehane called Texas 'the flagship' for the venture.
Newmark arranged $2.3 billion in financing for the 206 MW Abilene data center on behalf of Blue Owl Capital, Crusoe Energy Systems, and Primary Digital Infrastructure.

The Abilene Stargate site was expected to house 64,000 Nvidia GB200 chips by end of 2026, with an initial 16,000-chip deployment targeted for summer 2025; Oracle was reported to be in charge of operating the supercomputer.

In June 2025, Crusoe, Blue Owl Capital, and Primary Digital Infrastructure entered the second phase of a $15 billion joint venture for a 1.2 GW data center in Abilene; construction on six additional buildings began in March 2025, targeted to go live by mid-2026.

At a press conference in Abilene, OpenAI, Oracle, and SoftBank announced five new Stargate data center sites totaling 7 GW, including an additional 600 MW expansion near the original Abilene location.
Bloomberg reported that Oracle and OpenAI ended plans to expand the flagship Abilene data center amid financing complexity and revised demand assumptions.

Crusoe announced a 900 MW expansion of its Abilene AI campus as an 'AI Factory' for Microsoft, with behind-the-meter power generation and battery storage, bringing total planned campus capacity to approximately 2.1 GW.

Data Center Knowledge reported that Crusoe is adding a 900 MW AI data center to its Abilene campus for Microsoft, bringing total planned capacity to 2.1 GW, as part of a broader analysis of Texas becoming the largest data center market.

A Stargate progress report noted the 1,100-acre Abilene campus moved from groundworks to energization faster than comparable campuses but suffered weather-related outages; Microsoft partnered with Crusoe to develop additional buildings, transforming the site into a multi-tenant AI infrastructure hub.
Serena Energy's 265.5 MW Goodnight Wind farm came online in 2024 adjacent to the Goodnight campus site, Latitude Media reported, later becoming the basis for Crusoe's co-location proposal.
ABC7 Amarillo reported that construction on the Armstrong County data center began by Crusoe Energy in May 2025, with completion anticipated by late 2028 or early 2029.

In late October 2025, Crusoe and Goodnight Wind submitted a co-location (net metering) proposal to the Public Utility Commission of Texas under SB 6, seeking to share a single interconnection point between the 265.5 MW wind farm and the first phase of the data center, Latitude Media reported.

NewsChannel10 reported Armstrong County commissioners unanimously approved an amendment to Crusoe's tax abatement agreement, with the project scaled back from an original seven buildings on 350 acres to as few as three or four, and the county to receive $1.35 million per year per building in payments once each is operational.

Google CEO Sundar Pichai, alongside Governor Greg Abbott in Midlothian, announced a $40 billion Texas investment including a new data center in Armstrong County and two in Haskell County, the Texas Tribune reported.

ABC7 Amarillo reported Google's data center in Armstrong County will pull power off the ERCOT grid, use a closed-loop recirculating cooling system, and create 80 to 100 jobs, with Google serving as tenant, per County Judge Adam Ensey.

Crusoe Energy filed a 465-page application with TCEQ in January 2026 to build a 933 MW off-grid natural gas power plant at the Goodnight campus designed to power at least two buildings, which could emit up to 4.5 million tons of CO2 per year, exceeding San Francisco's entire annual emissions, Yahoo/The Guardian reported.
In mid-March 2026, Crusoe sold the wind-co-located portion of the Goodnight campus to Ensign Infrastructure, a Delaware-incorporated special purpose vehicle, Latitude Media reported.

NewsChannel10 reported a grass fire near Claude, sparked when a vehicle left County Road 19 and caught fire, spread to 251 acres, prompting evacuation of the data center about half a mile away and threatening five homes.

The Public Utility Commission of Texas adopted final net metering rules for co-located data centers of 75 MW or larger under SB 6, requiring mandatory emergency curtailment within 30 minutes and prohibiting co-located loads from demand response programs, Latitude Media reported on April 3.

Cleanview founder Michael Thomas reported that satellite imagery showed construction of Crusoe's 933 MW gas plant at the Goodnight campus was 'well underway,' calling it 'one of the first direct investments in fossil fuel infrastructure' by Google, as covered by Yahoo/The Guardian.

Yahoo/The Guardian reported that Crusoe filed in January 2026 to build a 933 MW on-site natural gas power plant at the Goodnight campus that could emit up to 4.5 million tons of CO2 per year, and that Google spokesperson Chrissy Moy said 'We don't have a contract in place for the plant in Texas.'

Construction Review Online reported the Goodnight campus (filed as GN DC1, LLC and internally called Project Llano) had grown to a $29 billion-plus, seven single-story-building project, with buildings 3 and 4 (about $500 million each) among those under construction and a nuclear-powered deployment targeted for 2027.
Cedar Rapids officials publicly confirmed that Google was the company behind the previously unnamed, proposed ~$576 million, 1,396-acre data center project on the city's southwest side.

The Cedar Rapids City Council approved a development agreement/urban renewal ordinance for Google's data center in the Big Cedar Industrial Center, setting terms including a minimum $576 million investment, construction start within three years, and at least 31 new full-time jobs.

Google held a celebration event in Cedar Rapids to officially confirm its data center project at Alliant Energy's Big Cedar Industrial Center and announced an additional $7 billion investment in Iowa over the next two years for cloud and AI infrastructure.

Google announced $7 billion in Iowa investment covering the new Cedar Rapids data center and expansion of its existing Council Bluffs facility, plus a workforce-development partnership with the electrical training ALLIANCE aimed at increasing Iowa's electrical workforce pipeline by 95%.

The Cedar Rapids City Council was set to vote on an indemnification agreement giving Google a temporary certificate of occupancy for the first data center building while impacts were evaluated — the concern centered on heat and steam plumes potentially interfering with landings at the nearby Eastern Iowa Airport.

Cedar Rapids Mayor Tiffany O'Donnell denied allegations that council members received kickbacks tied to the Google and QTS data center projects; reporting found the city manager and utilities business manager had signed NDAs with Google and QTS early in the projects' development.

Neighbors voiced concerns about 'Project Zodiac,' a proposed data center by an unnamed Fortune 100 company on southeast Fort Wayne land, following an October 25 neighborhood meeting; residents cited noise and health worries.
Allen County Plan Commission unanimously approved annexation of 728 acres of county land into Fort Wayne for the Project Zodiac data center; residents expressed frustration at the decision.
Allen County Commissioners voted 3-0 to approve the 728-acre Project Zodiac annexation near East Paulding Road and Adams Center Road, the final annexation vote required for the project.

Google was identified as the company behind 'Project Zodiac' at a groundbreaking ceremony in April 2024, announcing a $2 billion investment and approximately 200 jobs at the Fort Wayne data center campus.
IDEM held a public meeting on July 1 at Ivy Tech Community College to discuss the draft Hatchworks LLC air permit for Google's data center; the public comment period closed July 8.
Indiana Michigan Power and Google filed a joint demand-response contract with the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission to manage the data center's electricity load and grid impact.
Google filed an application with IDEM to build on approximately 2.47 acres of protected wetlands for Phase 2 of its Fort Wayne data center expansion.
IDEM approved Google's permit to build on approximately 2.5 acres of protected wetlands at the Fort Wayne data center site, requiring purchase of mitigation credits.

IDEM held a nearly three-hour public hearing at Ivy Tech on Google's request to expand from 34 to 179 backup diesel generators; the packed auditorium left more than 20 residents unable to speak, and attendees demanded the permit be denied.

Residents rallied at Indiana Michigan Power headquarters and Fort Wayne City Council, calling on the council to pressure IDEM to deny Google's diesel generator permit, citing potential annual pollution of 900 tons and rising energy costs.
IDEM approved AEP's request to temporarily fill wetlands to build power infrastructure serving Google's Fort Wayne data center.

Google announced its Fort Wayne data center is operational and held a community forum at Grand Wayne Center; the company pledged $1.2 million to ACRES Land Trust to protect 22 acres of wetlands and committed to using backup generators only for testing or emergencies.
Fort Wayne City Council reported that Google agreed to pay approximately $200,000 for stormwater drainage improvements at 6015 Adams Center Road near the data center campus.
Google launched a public website to address community questions and concerns about its Fort Wayne data center operations.
Indiana Michigan Power announced plans to lower electric rates, citing revenue from data centers including Google's Fort Wayne facility as an offset for residential customers.
Google filed permits with IDEM for Phase 3 of its Fort Wayne data center, proposing three additional buildings that would expand the campus footprint to over 867,000 square feet.
IDEM approved Google's request for 140 additional emergency diesel generators (plus 5 smaller units) at the Fort Wayne data center, on top of 34 already permitted in 2024.

Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission approved the Google-Indiana Michigan Power demand-response deal, allowing Google to curtail usage during peak grid stress in exchange for rate discounts, projected to reduce costs for all I&M customers.

Fort Wayne City Council member Russ Jehl introduced three resolutions demanding Google demonstrate compliance with tax-break benchmarks, accountability for land-sale proceeds directed to southeast Fort Wayne, and creation of a permanent data center oversight board.

Hatchworks LLC requested IDEM approval to fill 2.13 acres of forested wetlands for Phase 3, proposing a 2-to-1 mitigation ratio; a virtual public hearing is scheduled for August 25, 2026, with construction targeted to begin mid-September if approved.

The Stargate Project was announced at the White House as a $500 billion venture by SoftBank, OpenAI, Oracle, and MGX to build AI data center infrastructure in the United States, with SoftBank as financial lead and OpenAI as operational lead.

Foxconn announced the sale of its 6.2 million-square-foot former GM assembly plant in Lordstown to SoftBank for $375 million; the buyer was later identified as SoftBank's affiliate Crescent Dune LLC, a Delaware entity formed in July 2025.

Foxconn Chairman Young Liu announced a joint venture with SoftBank to manufacture AI data center equipment at the Lordstown plant, with Foxconn and SoftBank each holding 50% of the manufacturing operation while SoftBank owns the facility and equipment outright.

OpenAI, Oracle, and SoftBank announced five new Stargate data center sites including Lordstown, Ohio; SoftBank said it had already broken ground on an advanced data center at the site, with the facility on track to be operational in 2026.

Crescent Dune LLC (SoftBank affiliate) recorded the property transfer of the former GM Lordstown plant and nearly 600 acres from Foxconn EV Property Development LLC with the Trumbull County Auditor, listing a sale price of $88 million for the building and land.

Bristolville 25 Developer LLC, a separate New York-based developer, submitted a site plan proposal to Lordstown zoning for a $3.6 billion, 1.65 million-square-foot data center on 133 acres adjacent to the Stargate campus.

Preparation work began on the Lordstown Stargate data center, with crews clearing space in front of the former GM plant near the northwest corner along Hallock Young Road and dismantling a solar array near the former paint facility.

Lordstown Village Council voted 6-0 to ban all future data centers in the village, with approximately 100 residents attending and the majority speaking in opposition to data center development; the ban was set to take effect December 3.

Bristolville 25 Developer LLC and BHGH Properties LLC filed a petition for a writ of mandamus in the Ohio Supreme Court to compel Lordstown to accept, review, and act upon the developer's site plan submission under Ohio law.

Crescent Dune LLC filed wetland and stream delineation documents with the Ohio EPA for a 160-acre expansion behind the Lordstown plant for modular data center and server manufacturing, assembly for IT server racks, and related components.

Lordstown Village Council repealed its data center ban on the advice of the village solicitor, who stated Ohio courts favor moratoriums over outright bans; a public hearing on a replacement 180-day moratorium was scheduled for January 5, 2026.

The Ohio Supreme Court issued an entry denying Lordstown's motion to dismiss the Bristolville 25 mandamus case against the village and its zoning inspector, while granting dismissal of the village solicitor as a party; the court also granted an alternative writ.

Lordstown Village Council unanimously approved a 180-day moratorium on new data center permits after a public hearing attended by more than 50 residents, most of whom spoke against data centers; the moratorium was set to expire July 4, 2026.

Lordstown officials heard from land-use planner Brian Frantz, who advised the village to define data centers in zoning codes, designate appropriate locations, and use conditional-use permits to control placement, design, noise, and lighting.

Lordstown council approved a consulting agreement with planner Brian Frantz (not to exceed $7,625) for zoning and data center matters and advertised a public hearing to extend the data center moratorium for an additional 180 days.

Lordstown Village Council approved by emergency reading a 180-day extension of the data center moratorium, effective July 5, 2026 through January 2, 2027, to allow continued development of zoning standards for setbacks, noise, water usage, and other data center impacts.

projects.name: OpenAI Stargate Michigan
projects.note: Part of Stargate.

events.summary: Saline Township Board voted 4-1 to deny rezoning of 575 acres of agricultural land for Related Digital's proposed data center campus.
Related Digital sued Saline Township in Washtenaw County Circuit Court alleging exclusionary zoning barred by the Michigan Constitution, days after the board's rezoning denial.

Saline Township Board voted 4-1 to approve a consent agreement with Related Digital allowing the data center to proceed, including $4M farmland preservation trust, $2M community investment fund, $8M for fire services, and water protections.

Governor Whitmer announced that OpenAI and Oracle were behind the Saline Township data center, calling it the largest investment in Michigan history; the consent judgment was entered October 15, 2025.

DTE Energy filed an application with the Michigan Public Service Commission for fast-track approval of special electric service contracts to supply 1.4 GW to the data center, approximately 25% of DTE's entire load.

Approximately 100 people protested outside DTE Energy headquarters demanding transparency and a contested-case proceeding for the data center power contracts; speakers included Michigan Sierra Club and Washtenaw County Commissioner Yousef Rabhi.

Michigan Public Service Commission held a virtual public hearing on DTE's special electric service contracts for the 1.4 GW data center; AG Nessel called the hearing 'little more than performative listening.'

Saline Township resident Kathryn Haushalter, living 256 yards from the site, filed a motion to intervene in the consent judgment, alleging the settlement was negotiated in secret and violated Michigan's Open Meetings Act.
Michigan Public Service Commission granted conditional approval of DTE Energy's special contracts to supply power to the 1.4 GW Saline Township data center.
DTE Energy accepted the Michigan Public Service Commission's conditions for the Saline Township data center power contracts, while reserving rights to challenge future commission decisions.
Saline Township residents filed a separate mandamus complaint alleging the Zoning Board of Appeals failed to hold a required hearing on temporary structures permits for the data center.

Washtenaw County Circuit Judge Julia Owdiej denied resident Kathryn Haushalter's motion to intervene in the data center settlement, ruling it came too late; developer's attorney noted a $40M nonrefundable DTE deposit and $2B in equipment had been ordered.

In April 2026, Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel filed an appeal of the MPSC's conditional approval, contending the commission improperly fast-tracked approval without allowing a contested case proceeding.
Related Digital secured financing through Blackstone for the project, now valued at $16 billion, with major construction reported underway.
Saline Township Treasurer Jennifer Zink resigned after six years in office citing death threats linked to the data center project, which she had originally voted against as a board member.

Oracle, OpenAI, Related Digital, Blackstone, Walbridge, and Governor Whitmer held a groundbreaking ceremony for the Stargate campus nicknamed 'The Barn' in Saline Township; Sam Altman called it a 'huge bet' on AI.
Saline Township Board approved tax breaks for the data center but initially capped the abatement at $4.8 billion in valuation, smaller than the developer requested.

Saline Township Board voted 5-0 to reverse course and remove the $4.8 billion valuation cap on the data center tax abatement after the township attorney warned the cap would violate the 2025 consent judgment.
Oracle and OpenAI applied for a permit to discharge treated wastewater into the Saline River; Michigan EGLE opened a public comment period ending August 24.

AG Nessel, Earthjustice, Sierra Club, Michigan Environmental Council, and NRDC filed briefs with the Michigan Court of Appeals challenging the MPSC's approval of DTE's power contracts, arguing ratepayers face nearly half a billion dollars in up-front costs.

projects.name: OpenAI Stargate Milam
projects.note: Part of Stargate.

events.summary: President Trump announced the Stargate Project, a $500 billion AI infrastructure joint venture by OpenAI, SoftBank, and Oracle, with initial deployment in Texas.
Data Center Dynamics reported that solar power and battery storage systems are planned for the Stargate AI data center campus in Milam County.
Austin Business Journal reported a $3 billion data center campus planned in Milam County by SB Energy, before a tenant had been publicly identified.
The Real Deal reported that SB Energy's planned $3B Milam County data center was still searching for an end user and seeking tax breaks.
OpenAI, Oracle, and SoftBank announced an expansion of Stargate with five new AI data center sites across the U.S., including the Milam County, Texas campus.
Austin Business Journal reported that OpenAI would occupy the planned $3B Milam County data center hub as part of the Stargate project.
Austin Business Journal reported the OpenAI data center could create hundreds of jobs as part of a $135 million incentive deal in Milam County.

OpenAI and SoftBank Group each invested $500 million in SB Energy; OpenAI leased 1.2 GW of data center capacity for initial buildout in Milam County, Texas, with facilities expected to enter service starting in 2026.
Data Center Dynamics reported that SoftBank's SB Energy would build and operate OpenAI's 1.2 GW Stargate data center in Milam County, Texas.
Milam County Commissioners Court approved a tax abatement for a new data center, as reported by KXXV.
Austin Business Journal reported hints connecting a Silicon Valley company to the takeover of the old 3M campus in Milam County for data center use linked to Stargate.
MySA reported that data center developers made nearly $500 million in moves in Central Texas towns amid water concerns in the Milam County area.
Data Center Dynamics reported that OpenAI Stargate's Milam County 'Freebird' data center first phase would span 548,950 square feet.
The Texas Tribune reported that a Texas county paused data center construction in rural areas for one year, in response to rapid data center expansion in the region.
Austin Business Journal reported that one of the world's largest companies (linked to SoftBank) purchased approximately 4,700 acres in Milam County in a detail-sparse land transaction.
KCENTV reported that rock trucks driving through downtown Temple were traced to the $470 million OpenAI data center construction project in Milam County.
SB Energy committed to comply with Governor Abbott's data center transparency and accountability standards for Texas, alongside Core Scientific and Vantage Data Centers.

projects.name: OpenAI Stargate New Mexico
projects.note: Part of Stargate.

events.summary: Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham announced a partnership with BorderPlex Digital Assets to build a $5 billion digital infrastructure campus in Santa Teresa, expected to create 1,000 jobs — the first announcement of the site that would become Project Jupiter.

Dona Ana County Board of County Commissioners voted 4-1 to approve an ordinance authorizing issuance of up to $165 billion in Industrial Revenue Bonds for Project Jupiter, including an initial $50 billion investment within five years, a 30-year property-tax abatement offset by PILOT payments, $50 million for water/wastewater infrastructure, and a $6.9 million community investment fund.

TechCrunch reported OpenAI is building five new Stargate data centers with Oracle and SoftBank, bringing Stargate's planned capacity to 7 gigawatts; Dona Ana County, New Mexico was named as one of three new sites being developed with Oracle.

El Paso Matters reported OpenAI and Oracle had confirmed their partnership on the $165 billion Project Jupiter data center in Santa Teresa as part of the Stargate initiative, with $50 billion planned over five years, 2,500 construction jobs, and 750 permanent jobs.
Food and Water Watch reported that community members submitted over 7,000 comments to the New Mexico Environment Department regarding Project Jupiter's initial proposed gas plant (March 2026).

The Bureau of Land Management used emergency permitting authority to fast-track a construction review of the Green Chile natural gas pipeline, shortening the federal environmental review from about a year to 14 days; the ~18-mile, $60 million pipeline would carry 400 million cubic feet of gas per day to serve Project Jupiter.
The New Mexico Environment Department announced it would hold a public hearing on the air permit application for Project Jupiter's microgrid in response to community opposition (July 2026).

A Dona Ana County Commission meeting on Project Jupiter escalated into a physical confrontation: Commission Chair Manny Sanchez capped public comment at 30 speakers despite roughly 60 signed up; a Security Concepts guard pushed a woman to the ground, and she and two others were arrested. The guard was referred for potential felony assault charges, which prosecutors later declined to file.

projects.name: OpenAI Stargate Shackelford
projects.note: Part of Stargate.

events.summary: Shackelford County Commission unanimously approved Vantage Data Centers' 1,200-acre data center project, including a 10-year tax abatement with $10 million in annual payments to the county.

KTXS reported the Vantage data center is expected to create 250 full-time permanent jobs and employ up to 6,500 workers during peak construction, with construction starting later in 2025 and completion targeted for 2029.

Vantage Data Centers formally announced its $25 billion Frontier campus in Shackelford County: 1.4 GW of capacity across 10 data centers on 1,200 acres totaling 3.7 million square feet, with over 5,000 jobs expected across construction and operations.

CarbonCredits.com reported on water concerns around the Frontier campus, noting Texas Water Development Board forecasts that data centers could account for about 7 percent of Texas' total projected water use by 2030; Vantage had not disclosed specific water consumption projections for the site.

Vantage Data Centers broke ground on the Frontier campus, confirmed as part of OpenAI and Oracle's Stargate initiative; the first facility was scheduled for Q2 2026 with full campus completion targeted for 2028.

County Judge John M. Viertel held an informal open session with residents to discuss reinvestment zones after a second data center proposal was introduced at a commissioners court meeting; residents questioned whether another data center was necessary.

County Judge John Viertel acknowledged community backlash against the second proposed data center, stating 'the overall view is resistance' and that residents prioritize cultural preservation over economic benefits; water supply was cited as the most prominent concern.

A town hall was held at Albany High School for community input on a second data center proposed by Bolt Data and Energy at Buck Nail Ranch, about 16 miles west of Albany; the company had not disclosed the project's size, water demand, or job count, and commissioners had not approved the project.

KTXS reported mixed community reactions to the second proposed data center; resident Blaine Kayga said 'there's just way more negatives than there are positives,' citing traffic and safety issues from existing data center construction, while others noted potential employment benefits.

projects.name: OpenAI Stargate Wisconsin
projects.note: Part of Stargate.

events.summary: Port Washington's Common Council took up annexing and rezoning roughly one-third of the 1,900-acre project site from the Town of Port Washington for a data center then tied to Houston developer Cloverleaf, with town board and council meetings held that day on about 2,000 acres (~17% of the town).
Vantage Data Centers was identified as the operator for Port Washington's proposed data center campus, described as a 3.5-gigawatt project with a 1.3-gigawatt first phase targeted for 2027.

A Vantage official expressed concern in an email about the Wisconsin DNR's position that a full Environmental Impact Statement would be required for the Port Washington data center, according to records later cited in litigation.

The Port Washington Common Council unanimously approved a development agreement with Vantage Data Centers for an $8 billion, four-building data center campus and approved annexing nearly 700 more acres, bringing the total annexed to 1,315 of the 1,900-acre site.

A Vantage official texted the Port Washington mayor about the governor's office questioning why an Environmental Impact Statement would 'kill the project,' according to records cited in the Sierra Club/MEA lawsuit.

OpenAI, Oracle and Vantage Data Centers announced the 'Lighthouse' Stargate data center campus in Port Washington: a $15 billion investment for four data centers on 672 acres delivering close to a gigawatt of AI capacity, with a minimum $175 million in regional infrastructure upgrades and completion scheduled for 2028.
Three members of the opposition group Great Lakes Neighbors United were arrested at a Port Washington city council meeting in December 2025, according to later reporting.
Vantage held a groundbreaking ceremony marking the start of construction on the $15 billion Lighthouse data center campus in Port Washington, with the first phase to be completed in 2028.

The Metropolitan Milwaukee Association of Commerce (MMAC) sued the City of Port Washington seeking an injunction to block an April referendum that would require voter approval for TID-financed projects exceeding $10 million.

Great Lakes Neighbors United's lawsuit challenging the city's tax incremental district was reported, contending the TID provides property tax reimbursement and interest payments to the developer totaling more than $458 million over 18 years; the city moved to dismiss.

A recall petition against Port Washington Mayor Ted Neitzke, organized by Great Lakes Neighbors United, was submitted by the February 16 deadline but the city's initial review found it fell several hundred signatures short of the roughly 1,600-1,800 required.
A court denied MMAC's request to halt the Port Washington tax-incentive referendum, allowing the April ballot measure to proceed.

Port Washington neighbors pushed back on 24-hour weekday construction at Vantage's Lighthouse campus, submitting a 100-person petition to restore original hours and citing round-the-clock work lights and backup beeping, with the Planning Commission set to take up the issue.

Port Washington voters passed a referendum with 66% approval requiring voter approval before the city grants tax incentives exceeding $10 million to developers; organizers said the measure does not affect the current Vantage deal but restricts future data center tax breaks.
The Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources issued permits for the Vantage Port Washington data center project without preparing a full Environmental Impact Statement.

Midwest Environmental Advocates, on behalf of Sierra Club Wisconsin, sued the Wisconsin DNR in Ozaukee County Circuit Court, alleging the agency violated the Wisconsin Environmental Policy Act by issuing permits for the data center without a full Environmental Impact Statement.
Eagle Mountain City announced QTS had broken ground on a new data center campus situated west of the existing Meta facility, calling it a significant economic development win.

Eagle Mountain City reported that construction on the QTS data center campus had resumed after a brief delay to ensure the necessary energy infrastructure and resources were in place, citing an expected 2,000-3,000 temporary construction jobs and 100-200 permanent positions.
QTS and Layton Construction held a topping-out ceremony after placing the final structural beam on the first phase's third building, attended by about 2,000 construction workers.

A news report detailed the project: a 193-acre campus with an initial three buildings of 579,000-592,000 square feet each, backed by a $6 billion QTS investment, with a closed-loop cooling system needing only an initial water fill with no additional draw for cooling once operational.

KUTV reported that Utah House Bill 76, passed earlier in 2026, now requires large data centers to report water consumption, but the law applies only to facilities that become operational after July 2026 — potentially exempting already-approved projects.
